name: Leominster
headline: A city that once made combs,
with a state forest at its back door.
answer: Leominster is a city of 43,782 people (2020 Census) in northern Worcester County, just south of Fitchburg. Its housing includes worker cottages, three-deckers and duplexes from its comb and plastics years. Route 2 and I-190 pass through, and North Leominster station is on the MBTA Fitchburg Line to Boston's North Station.
overview: Leominster grew out of Lancaster. Permanent settlement began around 1725, the town was established in 1740, and it became a city in 1915. Its factories gave it a distinct story: comb shops lined Exchange Street in Morse Hollow, and after celluloid was invented in 1868 Leominster became known as the Comb City. Plastics followed, and the plastic pink flamingo lawn ornament was invented here in 1956. John Chapman, the orchard planter known as Johnny Appleseed, was born here in 1774; a marker stands on Johnny Appleseed Lane.

Monument Square has been the civic and commercial center since the 1800s, and the railroad has run through North Leominster since 1841, where the commuter rail station now sits on Nashua Street. Open land is close. Leominster State Forest offers swimming at Crow Hill Pond, the Crow Hill Ledges and a stretch of the Midstate Trail. Sholan Farms, bought with the city's help, grows apples, berries and pumpkins on Pleasant Street. Phase One of the Twin Cities Rail Trail now links the business districts of Leominster and Fitchburg.

Recent change in Leominster has come as much through infrastructure as through housing. Phase One of the Twin Cities Rail Trail, from Carter Park to First Street in Fitchburg, was completed by a bicycle and pedestrian bridge over Route 2, celebrated on August 3, 2024, and a $25 million second phase is planned to link downtown Leominster with Fitchburg's intermodal center. Heavy rain on September 11, 2023 caused significant flooding and a state of emergency. The state lists Leominster as compliant with the MBTA Communities law as of October 21, 2026. The city's ten-year tax rate history lists one rate per year, and that rate has fallen each year since FY2021, from $18.13 to $13.67 per $1,000 in FY2026.

housing.text: Single-family houses make up most of Leominster's residential parcels: for FY2026 the city's assessors counted 8,317 single-family parcels, 1,933 condominiums, 832 two-family and 334 three-family houses, and 327 apartment properties. The 2020 Census counted 18,732 housing units. The Massachusetts Historical Commission's 1984 survey records gable-end duplexes and double houses from the mid-1800s, a worker cottage and multifamily zone extending east from Whitney Street along Water, Spruce and Mechanic Streets, worker housing in Lincoln Terrace east of Central Street, and Queen Anne duplexes and three-deckers built in the early 1900s. The West Side, west of Main Street and north of West Street, and a hillside area around Merriam, Walnut, Winter and Grove Streets grew as residential districts in the 19th century.

name: Framingham
headline: Several old centers, one city,
on the road and rail line west of Boston.
answer: Framingham is a city of 72,362 people (2020 Census) in Middlesex County, on the main western corridor out of Boston. It grew from separate centers, including Saxonville, Framingham Centre and South Framingham, and its housing runs from mill-era double houses to two-families and suburban homes. Framingham station serves the Framingham/Worcester Line, and the Massachusetts Turnpike crosses the city.
overview: Framingham never had a single village at its heart. John Stone settled near the Sudbury River falls in 1647 and built a gristmill there, the start of what became the mill village of Saxonville. The town was incorporated in 1700, and Framingham Centre grew up as the civic focus on the old Boston turnpike. When the Boston and Worcester railroad reached South Framingham in 1834, that area became the industrial center. Voters approved a city charter in 2017, and Framingham became a city on January 1, 2018.

Those separate centers still shape the map. Saxonville keeps mid-1800s mill housing near the falls, and the Framingham Centre Common Historic District holds 28 buildings around the old common, including the Village Hall and First Parish Church. The Danforth Art Museum and School is now part of Framingham State University. Green space comes in several forms: Callahan State Park has more than 800 acres and seven miles of marked trails, Garden in the Woods shows New England native plants on 45 acres, and the Cochituate Rail Trail runs from Concord Street toward Natick.

Downtown, around the Concord Street common and the rail station, is where the city has zoned for denser housing. Town Meeting approved a Central Business (CB) district there in 2015, and in December 2024 the mayor submitted it to the state as Framingham's district under the MBTA Communities law. The state granted conditional compliance on January 22, 2025, and the city announced full compliance in July 2025; the state's compliance list, as of October 21, 2026, includes Framingham. Projects downtown include Alta Union House, 196 apartments across Concord Street from the Downtown Common, which was scheduled to open to tenants on July 24, 2019, and 181 homes at 358 Waverly Street, about 500 feet from the commuter rail station, where ground was broken in late 2025. The city's 2026 to 2030 Consolidated Plan records a call from stakeholders for more "missing middle" housing types.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission's survey of Framingham records central-chimney double houses built for mill workers at Saxonville around 1825 to 1835, wood-frame tenements and row houses in South Framingham and Coburnville, and two-family houses that were widely built there from about 1915 to 1940, a period with relatively few three-deckers. Larger suburban houses were built around Framingham Centre on Park Street, Prospect Street and Salem Road. The city's 2026 to 2030 Consolidated Plan counts 15,318 owner-occupied homes and 12,492 rental units, and 93 percent of the owner-occupied homes are single-unit houses. Seventy-seven percent of the housing stock was built before 1980, and the largest share, 21 percent, dates from 1950 to 1959 (American Community Survey, 2018 to 2022).

name: Marlborough
headline: A shoe-making city at the crossroads
of I-495 and I-290.
answer: Marlborough is a city of 41,793 people (2020 Census) in Middlesex County, where I-495 meets the eastern end of I-290. Its downtown grew from two 1800s shoe-making villages, and its housing includes three-deckers, double houses and converted factory condominiums. The city has no rail station; buses connect to Southborough and Framingham on the Framingham/Worcester Line.
overview: Families from Sudbury petitioned for a new town in 1656, and Marlborough was incorporated in 1660. The early settlement was largely destroyed during King Philip's War, then rebuilt along the Post Road, where George Washington stopped at Williams Tavern in 1789. Shoemaking defined the 1800s. Samuel and Joseph Boyd opened the first shoe business in 1836, factory output rose into the millions of dollars by 1865, and Marlborough incorporated as a city in 1890. Its land once also included today's Northborough, Southborough, Westborough, Berlin and Hudson.

Downtown took shape from two villages, an East Village along Main and Maple Streets and a West Village along Pleasant and Main, which grew together once the railroad ran between them. In 2014 the city created a 50-acre Downtown Village district to encourage mixed-use building, and some old shoe factories and churches nearby are now condominiums. The Assabet River Rail Trail heads north toward Hudson past an overlook above Fort Meadow Reservoir, and the 615-acre Desert Natural Area protects pitch pine and scrub forest on the Sudbury line.

Most of Marlborough's recent housing has been multifamily rental. The city's draft Marlborough Forward plan (March 2026) describes the existing stock as largely single-family homes built before 1990, and names the Green District in the Southwest Quadrant, with 235 units on 10.2 acres, and Alta French Hill on Lincoln Street among the projects that added hundreds of apartments. Downtown zoning currently limits buildings to four stories or 60 feet, and the plan recommends allowing five. It puts Marlborough at 10.83 percent on the state's Subsidized Housing Inventory, above the 10 percent threshold of Chapter 40B, while warning that expiring affordability restrictions could change that. Marlborough is on the state's list of communities compliant with the MBTA Communities multifamily zoning law, as of October 21, 2026.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission's survey of Marlborough records central-chimney Colonial houses, Greek Revival and Italianate side-hall houses and cottages, wood-frame row and double houses, and three-deckers and apartment houses in the West Village and along Mechanic Street, with Dutch Colonial and bungalow houses from the early 1900s. The city's economic development office lists former factories and churches converted to condominiums. The 2020 Census counted 17,547 housing units, 4.6 percent of them vacant. The draft Marlborough Forward plan (March 2026), citing American Community Survey estimates, reports that 56 percent of households own their homes and 44 percent rent, and that much of the stock is single-family homes built before 1990.

commute.text: Marlborough has no commuter rail station of its own; MWRTA bus routes connect to the Southborough and Framingham stations on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line. I-495, US Route 20 and Route 85 pass through the city, and I-290 has its eastern end here.

places.line: About 23 acres along Main Street from Mechanic Street to Bolton Street (Route 85), listed on the National Register in 1998, including the 1905 Beaux-Arts City Hall and the Old Common Cemetery of 1706.

places.line: About 260 acres on the Hudson line, with Memorial Beach on the Marlborough side and Centennial Beach on the Hudson side; motorized boating is allowed.

Attacked in March during King Philip's War; the settlement was nearly destroyed.
George Washington stopped at Williams Tavern soon after his inauguration.

Incorporated as the City of Marlborough.

name: Wakefield
headline: A lake to walk around,
a town to come home to.
answer: Wakefield is a Middlesex County town about 10 miles north of Boston, centered on Lake Quannapowitt and a downtown along Main Street. Single-family detached homes make up 55 percent of its housing, and about a third of its structures predate World War II. The Haverhill Line stops at Wakefield and Greenwood stations.
overview: Wakefield is a town of about 27,000 people, 10 miles north of Boston, and it is laid out around Lake Quannapowitt. A paved loop of about 3.6 miles circles the lake, and Wakefield Common sits at its southern end. From there, downtown runs south along Main Street toward Crystal Lake, the town's drinking-water reservoir. The town began as part of Reading. Its South Parish broke off as South Reading in 1812, and in 1868 the town took the name of Cyrus Wakefield, who gave land and money for a new town hall.

Two Haverhill Line stations, Wakefield and Greenwood, serve the town, and I-95/Route 128 runs along its northwest edge. Greenwood covers nearly all of southern Wakefield, while Montrose, Woodville and Lakeside fill in the east and north. On Saturdays from June through October, the farmers market sets up on North Avenue by Hall Park, on the lake's shore. Breakheart Reservation, a state park with two lakes and a swimming beach at Pearce Lake, has an entrance on Hemlock Road, the one closer to the beach.

Wakefield's current housing plan, the Housing Production Plan for FY2026-2030, was adopted by the Town Council on June 23, 2025 and by the Planning Board on July 15, 2025, and is awaiting state certification. Under the state's MBTA Communities law, which places Wakefield in the commuter rail category, Town Meeting turned down three proposed multifamily districts in April 2024, then approved multifamily zoning districts and the matching bylaw change on November 16, 2024; the state's list as of October 21, 2026 shows Wakefield as compliant. The largest project under way is The Basin at 200 Quannapowitt, where Cabot, Cabot & Forbes began demolition in May 2023 for four buildings that the developer says will hold more than 440 apartments: the first, with 64 units, opened in August 2025, and the last, with 86 units, was scheduled for the second quarter of 2026. A town master plan, drafted with MAPC on the foundation of the earlier Vision 2030, is still being refined.

housing.text: The town's Housing Production Plan for FY2026-2030 reports that single-family detached homes are 55 percent of all housing units, down from 62 percent in 2011, and that about a third of structures were built before World War II. Two-family homes, buildings of 20 to 49 units, and three- and four-unit buildings are the next most common types. The plan was adopted by the Town Council on June 23, 2025 and the Planning Board on July 15, 2025.

commute.text: The Haverhill Line stops at Wakefield and Greenwood on the way to North Station, and MBTA bus route 137 also serves the town. I-95/Route 128 runs along the northwest border with exits in town, Route 129 runs through as Main Street, and the town notes that it sits near the junction of I-93 and I-95/128.

places.name: Wakefield Common

places.line: The public library at Main and Avon Streets downtown, opened in 1923.

places.line: About seven acres of late 18th- and early 19th-century houses on Church Street, just south of the lake, and Greek Revival houses on Lafayette Street, laid out in 1824; listed on the National Register in 1989.

places.line: The former West Ward School, a one-room schoolhouse that now houses the Wakefield Historical Society.

history.text: Incorporated as part of the town of Reading, after first settlement in 1638 as Lynn Village.
The South Parish separated from Reading and was incorporated as South Reading on February 25.
The railroad between Wilmington and Boston was chartered and built through town; it later became part of the Boston and Maine main line.
Cyrus Wakefield founded the Rattan Works, which grew into the Wakefield Rattan Company, at one time employing a thousand people.
Renamed Wakefield after Cyrus Wakefield donated land and money for a new town hall.

name: Reading
headline: A town common, a commuter line,
and woods a short walk from the front door.
answer: Reading is a Middlesex County town of 25,518 people (2020 Census) whose housing is mostly single-family, with a large share built before 1960. It grew around a traditional New England common and keeps conservation land such as the Town Forest. Reading station on the MBTA Haverhill Line runs to Boston's North Station, and I-93 and I-95/Route 128 cross the town.
overview: Reading began as an inland plantation for settlers from Lynn and was incorporated in 1644. Over the next two centuries it gave up land to form its neighbors: the parish to the south became South Reading and was renamed Wakefield in 1868, and the land north of the Ipswich River became North Reading in 1853. What remains centers on the Common, where Main and Salem Streets meet, framed by the First Congregational Church, the public library and the town hall.

The railroad reached Reading in 1845, and Woburn Street shows what followed: Queen Anne and Colonial Revival houses on well-proportioned lots along a tree-lined stretch, now a historic district. Around the built-up streets, Reading keeps a web of conservation land, from the Town Forest, its largest, to Bare Meadow and the Aberjona River Headwaters Trail through the Maillet Conservation Area.

Downtown Reading has been zoned for housing above and beside its shops since November 2009, when the town adopted a Downtown Smart Growth District under the state's Chapter 40R; Town Meeting added about 21 acres to it in 2017. Projects approved under 40R include Oaktree on Haven Street, the first built in the district, with 53 units over ground-floor retail, Postmark Square, which turned the historic post office into 50 ownership units, and 55 units at 20-24 Gould Street, completed in 2021. A second 40R district, the Gateway Smart Growth District, adopted in December 2007 at the southern town line, takes in 200 of the 424 units of Reading Woods, built on a former Addison-Wesley commercial site. In November 2024 Town Meeting approved zoning under the state's MBTA Communities law covering downtown and a smaller area near Summit Towers, and the state lists Reading as compliant.

housing.text: Reading's 2023 Housing Production Plan describes the housing stock as primarily single-family, at 76.7% of units, with 84.6% owner occupied. Over half of the homes were built before 1960, and about a third before 1940. The downtown area holds a number of multi-family, affordable and public housing developments.

name: Melrose
headline: Three train stops, one pond in the middle,
and Victorian streets that lead to the Fells.
answer: Melrose is a Middlesex County city of 29,817 people (2020 Census), about seven miles north of Boston. More than half its homes predate World War II, many Victorian near downtown and the rail line. Three MBTA Haverhill Line stations serve the city, and Oak Grove on the Orange Line sits just over the Malden border.
overview: Melrose was part of Charlestown and then Malden before it was incorporated as a town in 1850. When the Boston and Maine Railroad built three stops through it in 1845, houses followed the tracks, and in 1853 the town annexed the highlands from Stoneham. It became a city at the turn of the century, and its first mayor, Levi S. Gould, took office on January 1, 1900. Its downtown, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982, runs along Main Street, and Ell Pond, the city's largest body of water, sits near the center with a gazebo and a new fountain.

The housing tells the city's history in layers. A 2022 housing plan found that most homes built before World War II cluster near downtown and the rail corridor, often in Victorian styles, while the eastern side filled in after the war with ranches and Capes. Larger buildings are concentrated downtown and along Main Street. At the edges are big green spaces: the eastern reaches of the Middlesex Fells, the Olmsted-designed Pine Banks Park on the Malden line, and Mount Hood, a city park and golf course with views toward Boston.

Melrose meets the state's MBTA Communities law, as a commuter rail community, through zoning it already had: the Rail Corridor Overlay District, the Smart Growth Overlay District, the Urban Residential-D district and the Medical Business district, with a few minor amendments. The state lists it as compliant, as of October 21, 2026. Since 2004 the city's Affordable Housing Incentive Program ordinance has required certain residential and mixed-use projects to set aside 15 percent of their units as affordable to households earning up to 80 percent of the Boston-area median income. The city's affordable housing office lists affordable rentals created this way in projects including the Windsor Radio Factory at 99 Washington Street (19 affordable units, offered by lottery in 2022), The Washingtons at 2 and 37/47 Washington Street (17, lotteries in 2015 and 2016) and Jack Flats at 1000 Stone Place (19, lotteries in 2013 and 2014).

housing.text: Melrose's 2022 Housing Production Plan reports that 55% of homes are detached single-family and 11% are two-family, with 16% in buildings of 20 or more units. Over half were built before World War II, often in Victorian styles near downtown and the rail corridor; the eastern parts of the city saw more mid-century ranch and Cape houses after the war.

name: Stoneham
headline: A shoe town's square, a zoo by the pond,
and a third of the map left to the Fells.
answer: Stoneham is a Middlesex County town of 23,244 people (2020 Census), less than 10 miles northwest of Boston. About a third of its land lies in the Middlesex Fells Reservation. Slightly more than half its homes are single-family. I-93 runs through town, and Boston-bound rail stations sit in Melrose, Winchester and Malden next door.
overview: Early explorers called this land Charlestown End, and Governor Winthrop's party is said to have lunched by Spot Pond in 1632. Farmers settled slowly, and the town broke from Charlestown on December 17, 1725. A stagecoach line on the Medford to Andover Turnpike in 1833 brought house lots, and shoemaking grew from home workshops into more than forty manufacturers. That era left Central Square, with its Second Empire commercial blocks, the 1904 library, and churches lining the north side at Common Street.

A few blocks west of the square, Nobility Hill keeps Italianate, Stick and Queen Anne houses from about 1860 to 1920. The Middlesex Fells covers roughly a third of the town, with Spot Pond, Bear Hill and the Stone Zoo, founded in 1905. Stoneham's housing plan counts slightly more than half its homes as single-family, with much of the rest in larger buildings. The Tri-Community Greenway runs from Gould Street toward Woburn and Winchester.

Much of the Fells land in Stoneham was shaped by the Boston area's water supply. Spot Pond was enlarged into a storage reservoir for communities north of Boston, its level raised by 16 feet, and the Metropolitan District Commission replaced several town pumping stations with a single pumping station and gatehouse, listed on the National Register in 1984. Bear Hill Reservoir, just west of I-93 near the summit of Bear Hill, was built in 1902 and 1903 with two concrete dams and a gatehouse. Spot Pond is no longer part of the drinking water supply, and the John Botume House, a 19th-century granite house on its eastern shore, now serves as the reservation's visitor center.

housing.text: Stoneham's Housing Production Plan reports that 57.1% of housing units are single-family homes, and nearly half of the remaining multifamily units are in buildings of 20 or more units. About 65% of homes are owner-occupied. The plan points to the town center around Main Street as the area best suited for new housing.

commute.text: Stoneham has no rail station of its own; commuter rail stations in Melrose, Winchester, Wakefield and Woburn serve Boston's North Station, and Oak Grove on the Orange Line is about 3.8 miles from Stoneham Center. I-93 runs through town, I-95/Route 128 passes just to the north, and MBTA bus 132 runs between Redstone Shopping Center and Malden Center Station.

name: Lowell
headline: Brick mills, working canals,
and a city still built around its river.
answer: Lowell is a Middlesex County city of 115,554 people (2020 Census), founded as a textile mill town and incorporated in 1826. Most of its housing was built before 1960, with a mix of multi-family buildings, duplexes, single-family homes and converted mills. The MBTA Lowell Line runs from Lowell station to Boston's North Station, and I-495 and US-3 cross the city.
overview: The first large textile mill went up in 1822 on land that would become Lowell, and the town of Lowell was incorporated on March 1, 1826, then chartered as a city in 1836. By the 1850s it had the largest industrial complex in the United States. Much of that landscape survives: Lowell National Historical Park, created in 1978, runs boat tours through the canal system and recreates 19th-century textile work in the Boott Cotton Mills Museum. Along the river, the Vandenberg Esplanade is part of the state's Lowell Heritage State Park.

Lowell's neighborhoods differ widely. Downtown, the Acre and Back Central hold most of the city's rental housing, while parts of Belvidere, Pawtucketville and the Highlands are mostly single-family streets. Beyond the mill core, the Lowell-Dracut-Tyngsboro State Forest, shared with two neighboring towns, adds about six miles of trails.

Lowell's zoning ordinance dates to 2004, and the city is rewriting it, with Community Scale, Levine Planning Strategies and BBHS Law as consultants; a public forum on data centers in June 2026 was part of that work. The Hamilton Canal District, 15 acres of vacant and underused waterfront land downtown, is governed by a form-based code that the City Council adopted on February 24, 2009, following a 2008 master plan, with Trinity Financial as master developer. As a Gateway City, Lowell offers the state's Housing Development Incentive Program, a tax exemption and credit for market-rate housing created by substantial rehabilitation, and its 2024 to 2028 Housing Production Plan credits conversions of downtown buildings and mills with much of the city's recent production. The state lists Lowell as compliant with the MBTA Communities law, as of October 21, 2026.

housing.text: Lowell's Housing Production Plan for 2024 to 2028 reports that 77% of the city's housing was built before 1960, with nearly a third predating 1900, and that 45% of units are in buildings of three or more units. Conversions of downtown buildings and mills account for much of recent production, and parts of Belvidere, Pawtucketville and the Highlands are predominantly single-family.

places.line: A National Park Service site created in 1978, with the Boott Cotton Mills Museum, canal boat tours and the Mogan Cultural Center.

places.line: A DCR park established in 1974 that includes the riverside Vandenberg Esplanade.

places.line: More than 1,000 acres across three towns, with about six miles of trails, ponds and wetlands, entered from Trotting Park Road.

places.line: The circa 1825 house at 243 Worthen Street where James McNeill Whistler was born in 1834, now run by the Lowell Art Association.

places.line: A free festival held downtown on the last full weekend of July, with stages at Boarding House Park and along Market Street.

places.name: Pollard Memorial Library
places.line: Designed by Frederick W. Stickney and built in 1890 and 1891 as Memorial Hall, renamed in 1981 and renovated in the mid-2000s.

places.line: A converted mill at 122 Western Avenue with studios for more than 300 working artists and musicians.

places.name: Pawtucket Falls
places.line: A mile-long set of rapids with a total drop of about 32 feet, which powered the city's 19th-century industry.

The Boston & Lowell Railroad began service.

name: Newton
headline: Learn the villages first,
then find the street that fits.
answer: Newton is a city of thirteen villages in Middlesex County, about eight miles west of downtown Boston. Much of its housing is older: as of the 2000 Census, only 19 percent of its homes had been built after 1960. The Green Line D branch and the Framingham/Worcester commuter rail line connect it to Boston.
overview: Newton sits about eight miles west of downtown Boston and has no single center. Instead it is a patchwork of thirteen villages, from Auburndale and Waban to Nonantum and Chestnut Hill, and many of them have a small downtown of their own. The villages have no legal boundaries, so addresses can puzzle first-time visitors. The city goes by The Garden City. It began as Cambridge Village in 1681, took the name Newton in 1766 and became a city in 1874.

Water and transit shape the map. The Charles River runs along the city's north and west sides, past Newton Lower Falls and Newton Upper Falls, both former small industrial sites, and under Echo Bridge at Hemlock Gorge. The Green Line D branch runs through the middle of the city, with stops including Newton Centre and Riverside, while the Framingham/Worcester Line stops at Newtonville, West Newton and Auburndale. Commonwealth Avenue carries the Boston Marathon over Heartbreak Hill, between Walnut Street and Boston College.

Most of Newton's land is residential: in the city's FY2026 classification hearing packet, residential property made up 92.23 percent of taxable value, and 16,947 of its 26,888 residential parcels were single-family homes, alongside 5,883 condominiums and 2,490 two-family houses. The largest planned housing site is Riverside, the Green Line terminus, where the MBTA approved an 85-year lease of part of the parking lots for mixed-use development in 2009 and the city rezoned the site for a larger project in late 2019. A revised two-phase plan put to the MBTA board in August 2024 calls for about 545 apartments and a garage in the first phase, and an office or lab building of about 150,000 square feet with about 100 more units in the second. Under the state's MBTA Communities law, Newton appears on the state's list of compliant municipalities.

housing.text: A 2003 city survey of mid-20th-century housing reported that, as of the 1960 Census, 70.5 percent of Newton's housing units were single-family dwellings and 20.5 percent were two-family homes. It also noted that, as of the 2000 Census, only 19 percent of the city's dwellings had been built after 1960. The 2020 Census counted 33,320 housing units in the city. In the FY2026 assessment, 16,947 of 26,888 residential parcels were single-family, 5,883 were condominiums, 2,490 two-family, 252 three-family and 159 apartment buildings.

villages.name: Newton Centre
villages.line: Newton's largest village downtown, a triangle of shops around Beacon Street, Centre Street and Langley Road, with the Green Line station on Union Street and Crystal Lake, a 33-acre natural lake, in the village.

villages.name: Newtonville
villages.line: A commuter suburb that grew after the railroad arrived in 1834, with its center along Walnut Street, a Framingham/Worcester Line stop, and a Star Market built on air rights over the Massachusetts Turnpike.

villages.name: West Newton
villages.line: Northern village with a Framingham/Worcester Line stop; its village center along Washington Street is a National Register district, and West Newton Hill and Webster Park are historic residential districts listed in 1986.

villages.name: Auburndale
villages.line: Western village on the Charles River, split by the Turnpike, with a commuter rail stop, Lasell University, the Plummer Memorial Library and a local historic district of about 275 properties established in 2005; Norumbega Park operated here until 1963.

villages.name: Newton Upper Falls
villages.line: Mill village on the Charles River, where Newton's first mill was built in 1688; about 60 acres between Route 9 and Elliot Street form a National Register district listed in 1986, and Eliot station on the Green Line serves it.

villages.name: Newton Highlands
villages.line: A village platted as a commuter suburb after the Charles River Railroad was built in 1852, with late 19th-century houses, a historic district around its center, and Newton Highlands and Eliot stations on the Green Line D branch.

commute.text: The Framingham/Worcester commuter rail line stops at three northern villages, and the Green Line D branch runs through the city's center to Riverside. The Massachusetts Turnpike crosses the northern villages, and I-95/Route 128 runs along the western edge near Lower Falls.

places.name: Crystal Lake
places.line: A natural lake in Newton Centre with a city-run swim beach, bathhouse and summer lifeguards.

places.name: Jackson Homestead and Museum
places.line: Historic Newton's museum at 527 Washington Street, with exhibits on city history and the Underground Railroad.

places.name: Hammond Pond Reservation
places.line: A DCR reservation off Hammond Pond Parkway with trails, rock formations to climb and paddling on the pond.

places.name: Hemlock Gorge Reservation
places.line: A 23-acre DCR reservation on the Charles River, known for Echo Bridge and its echo.

places.name: Heartbreak Hill
places.line: The Boston Marathon's climb on Commonwealth Avenue between Walnut Street and Boston College.

places.name: Auburndale Cove
places.line: A picnic and recreation area on the Charles River in Auburndale.

places.name: Bullough's Pond
places.line: A former mill pond in Newtonville, reshaped as a landscape feature in the late 19th century, near the Johnny Kelley statue at the start of Heartbreak Hill.

places.name: West Newton Cinema
places.line: A Washington Street movie house opened in 1937 and expanded to six screens in 1990; a fundraising campaign reached its $5.6 million goal in August 2024 to keep it open.

history.text: Incorporated as a town under the name Cambridge Village, on December 15.
Took the name Newton, after being called Newtown from 1691.
The Boston and Worcester Railroad reached West Newton, starting the suburban growth of the northern villages.
Incorporated as a city on January 5.
The Highland branch railroad, closed in 1958, reopened in July 1959 as the Green Line D branch, with Newton Centre station back in service on July 4.

faq.a: Yes. The MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line stops at Newtonville, West Newton and Auburndale. The Green Line D branch also runs through the city, with stops including Newton Centre and Riverside.

name: Quincy
headline: Between the harbor and the hills,
a city with deep roots.
answer: Quincy is a coastal city in Norfolk County, on Boston Harbor, and the birthplace of John Adams and John Quincy Adams. About a third of its homes are detached single-family houses, and most of the rest are in buildings with two or more units. Four Red Line stations and three commuter rail lines connect it to Boston.
overview: Quincy calls itself the City of Presidents, and the reason is on Franklin Street: the houses where John Adams was born in 1735 and John Quincy Adams in 1767 still stand side by side there. The family's later home, the Old House at Peacefield, and its Stone Library are part of Adams National Historical Park. Quincy split from Braintree as a town in 1792 and became a city in 1888. Granite quarrying was its major industry for more than a century, and in 1826 the Granite Railway carried stone for the Bunker Hill Monument.

The shoreline runs from Squantum and Marina Bay around to Houghs Neck, with Wollaston Beach stretching about 2.3 miles along Quincy Shore Drive. Inland, the Blue Hills Reservation covers roughly a quarter of the city's land, and the old quarries in West Quincy are now a state reservation that climbers use. Four Red Line stations, North Quincy, Wollaston, Quincy Center and Quincy Adams, connect the city to Boston, and the Kingston, Greenbush and Fall River/New Bedford commuter rail lines all stop at Quincy Center.

Quincy permitted 3,008 units from 2015 through 2021, most of them in multifamily and mixed-use buildings, according to Housing Quincy, the 2022 MAPC study. Its zoning allows multifamily housing by right or by special permit in every district except Residential A, which is limited to single-family homes, and two special districts are aimed at transit: the Quincy Center districts and a transit-oriented district at North Quincy station. Projects of ten or more units that need a special permit, variance or site plan approval must set aside at least 10 percent of units as affordable, or donate land or pay a fee instead. Quincy Center has been the focus of an Urban Revitalization and Development Plan since 2007, covering 62 acres around the MBTA station, and the city began a Wollaston Urban Revitalization District in early 2021. The state lists Quincy as compliant with the MBTA Communities law.

housing.text: Housing Quincy, a 2022 study by the Metropolitan Area Planning Council, found that about a third of the city's housing units are detached single-family homes, two-thirds are in buildings with two or more units, and 63 percent were built after 1940. It describes the oceanfront areas of Squantum, Merrymount, Adams Shore and Houghs Neck as having predominantly older single-family housing. The same study found that 54 percent of occupied units are rented, and the 2020 Census counted 51,156 housing units in the city.

villages.name: Quincy Center
villages.line: The historic commercial and government center, with City Hall, the Thomas Crane Public Library, United First Parish Church and the city's main Red Line and commuter rail station.

villages.name: Wollaston
villages.line: Named for Captain Richard Wollaston, an early rail commuter neighborhood that is now densely built, with its own Red Line station; the city began the Wollaston Urban Revitalization District in early 2021.

villages.name: North Quincy
villages.line: A residential and commercial neighborhood along Hancock Street and Quincy Shore Drive, with a Red Line station at Hancock and Hunt Streets and a transit-oriented zoning district around it.

villages.name: Squantum
villages.line: The northernmost peninsula, once a summer seaside resort and now year-round, with mostly older single-family homes.

villages.name: Marina Bay
villages.line: Waterfront area developed in the 1980s on the former Naval Air Station Squantum, with high-rise condominiums, restaurants and a large marina.

villages.name: Houghs Neck
villages.line: Peninsula at the city's northeastern end, named for Atherton Hough, who was granted the land in 1636, with mostly older single-family homes.

commute.text: Quincy Center is a stop on three commuter rail lines and the Red Line, which has three more stations in the city. I-93 and US Route 1 run together through Quincy, joined by Route 3 at the Braintree Split, where the road becomes the Southeast Expressway.

places.name: Adams National Historical Park
places.line: The Adams birthplaces on Franklin Street, the Old House at Peacefield and its Stone Library.

places.name: Wollaston Beach and Quincy Shores Reservation
places.line: About 2.3 miles of beach along Quincy Shore Drive, with Caddy Park and a jogging and biking path.

places.name: Quincy Quarries Reservation
places.line: Inactive granite quarries where large-scale American quarrying began, now used for hiking and top-rope climbing.

places.name: Blue Hills Reservation
places.line: More than 7,000 acres and 125 miles of trails, stretching from Quincy to Dedham and from Milton to Randolph.

places.name: Thomas Crane Public Library
places.line: The main library, designed by H. H. Richardson and completed in 1882, is a National Historic Landmark.

places.name: United First Parish Church
places.line: The 1828 Greek Revival church at 1306 Hancock Street, designed by Alexander Parris and built of local granite; John Adams, John Quincy Adams and their wives are interred in its basement crypt. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1970.

places.name: Squantum Point Park
places.line: A DCR waterfront park on Victory Road, on a former Naval airfield, with paved accessible trails and views of the harbor and the Boston skyline.

places.name: Faxon Park
places.line: A wooded, 66-acre protected park in South Quincy.

history.text: Incorporated as the Town of Quincy, separated from Braintree and named for Col. John Quincy.
The Granite Railway was built to carry Quincy granite for the Bunker Hill Monument.
The Old Colony Railroad opened through Quincy, beginning its growth as a suburb.
Incorporated as a city.
Quincy Center station opened on September 1, when the Red Line was extended into Quincy (it reached Braintree in 1980); Old Colony commuter rail service resumed in 1997.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Quincy, MA?
faq.a: For calendar year 2025, The Warren Group reports a single-family median sale price of $706,250 in Quincy, across 418 sales. In 2024 the median was $700,000 on 364 sales. Source: The Warren Group, MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town.

faq.q: Does Quincy have commuter rail?
faq.a: Yes. The MBTA Kingston, Greenbush and Fall River/New Bedford lines stop at Quincy Center. The Red Line also serves North Quincy, Wollaston, Quincy Center and Quincy Adams.

faq.q: Which school district serves Quincy?
faq.a: Quincy Public Schools. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Quincy, MA?
faq.a: For fiscal year 2026, Quincy's rates are $11.78 per $1,000 of assessed value for residential property and $23.53 per $1,000 for commercial property, according to the city assessors. In fiscal 2025 they were $11.53 and $23.01.

faq.q: Is there a beach in Quincy?
faq.a: Yes. Wollaston Beach runs about 2.3 miles along Quincy Shore Drive and is part of the state's Quincy Shores Reservation.

faq.q: What kinds of housing are being built in Quincy?
faq.a: Quincy permitted 3,008 housing units from 2015 through 2021, most of them in multifamily and mixed-use buildings, according to MAPC's 2022 Housing Quincy study. Projects of ten or more units that need a special permit, variance or site plan approval must set aside at least 10 percent of units as affordable, or donate land or pay a fee instead.

name: Springfield
headline: Porches, parks and river light,
in a city that knows its neighborhoods.
answer: Springfield is the seat of Hampden County, on the eastern bank of the Connecticut River about 24 miles north of Hartford. Sixty-eight percent of its housing is single-family homes and duplexes, and 41 percent was built before 1940. Union Station offers Amtrak and Hartford Line trains, and I-91 and I-291 run through the city.
overview: Springfield sits on the eastern bank of the Connecticut River, about 24 miles north of Hartford, and serves as the Hampden County seat. William Pynchon founded it in 1636 as Agawam Plantation, and it became a city in 1852. The federal armory here began making small arms in 1794 and closed in 1968; its Main Arsenal now holds the National Park Service's collection of historic military firearms. James Naismith invented basketball in Springfield in 1891, and the Hall of Fame stands on the riverfront.

The city calls itself the City of Homes, a name tied to its Victorian houses. The McKnight Historic District, planned in 1881, has more than 900 of them, and the neighborhood around Forest Park has more than 600. Sixteen Acres holds much of the city's post-World War II building, and Indian Orchard grew up as its own mill town on the Chicopee River. Forest Park covers about 735 acres, with a zoo, Porter Lake and the Bright Nights holiday display. Union Station handles Amtrak, Hartford Line trains and intercity buses.

The city's 2018 Housing Study counted 61,851 housing units and a homeownership rate of 47 percent, and it reported that the city had focused new construction and rehabilitation in Old Hill, Six Corners, the South End and Memorial Square, neighborhoods hit hard by the foreclosure crisis; it proposed keeping those four and Brightwood as Neighborhood Revitalization Strategy Areas. Many of the homes built in late 2011 and 2012 replaced ones destroyed by the tornado of June 1, 2011, which hit the South End hard. Downtown changed in the late 2010s: Union Station reopened on June 24, 2017 after restoration, Hartford Line trains began serving it on June 16, 2018, and MGM Springfield opened in Metro Center on August 24, 2018. Springfield lies outside the MBTA system and does not appear on the state's MBTA Communities compliance list.

housing.text: The city's 2018 Housing Study found that 68 percent of Springfield's housing stock is single-family homes and duplexes, and that only 10 percent of units are in buildings with 20 or more units. It also found that 41 percent of units were built before 1940 and only 14 percent since 1980. The study counted 61,851 housing units (2016 ACS), with single-family homes alone making up 44 percent and a homeownership rate of 47 percent.

villages.name: Forest Park
villages.line: Residential district around the 735-acre park of the same name, including the Forest Park Heights Historic District with more than 600 Victorian houses.

villages.name: McKnight
villages.line: Primarily residential; its historic district, planned in 1881, has more than 900 Victorian houses.

villages.name: Six Corners
villages.line: Urban and residential, including Mulberry Street in the Ridgewood Historic District.

villages.name: Sixteen Acres
villages.line: Suburban in character, with much of the city's post-World War II housing.

villages.name: Indian Orchard
villages.line: Former mill town on the Chicopee River that grew separately before joining Springfield; some of its mill buildings now hold artists' spaces, and Lake Lorraine State Park is here.

villages.name: Metro Center
villages.line: Downtown, separated from the Connecticut River riverfront by I-91.

rail.line: Amtrak (Northeast Regional, Valley Flyer, Vermonter, Lake Shore Limited)

commute.text: Springfield has no MBTA commuter rail. Union Station on Frank B. Murray Street serves Amtrak, the CTrail Hartford Line to New Haven, PVTA local buses and Peter Pan intercity buses. I-91 follows the riverfront, I-291 loops northeast from downtown to the Massachusetts Turnpike, and the Turnpike itself runs just north of the city through Chicopee.

places.name: Forest Park
places.line: About 735 acres, established in 1884, with the Zoo at Forest Park, Porter Lake and the Bright Nights holiday display.

places.name: Springfield Museums
places.line: Five museums of art, history, science and Dr. Seuss at 21 Edwards Street, including the Springfield Science Museum.

places.name: Springfield Armory National Historic Site
places.line: The nation's first armory, now a National Park Service site holding a large collection of historic US military small arms.

places.name: Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame
places.line: The Hall of Fame at 1000 Hall of Fame Avenue, beside the Connecticut River, in a building opened in 2002.

places.name: Springfield Union Station
places.line: The 1926 station, redeveloped as the city's rail and bus hub on Frank B. Murray Street.

places.name: Court Square
places.line: The civic center on Main Street, ringed by historic buildings, with monuments to Miles Morgan and President William McKinley; Old First Church, an 1819 rebuilding of the 1638 congregation's church, stands on it.

places.name: Stearns Square
places.line: A downtown square designed in 1897 by Stanford White and Augustus Saint-Gaudens, at the center of the Club Quarter.

places.name: Symphony Hall
places.line: Part of the Springfield Municipal Group, dedicated in 1913, and home of the Springfield Symphony Orchestra.

history.text: Founded by William Pynchon as Agawam Plantation.
During Shays' Rebellion, insurgents nearly captured the armory, an episode that helped lead to the U.S. Constitutional Convention.
The armory, an arsenal since the Revolutionary War, began making muskets; it closed in 1968 and reopened as a National Historic Site in 1978.
Incorporated as a city on May 25.
James Naismith invented basketball in Springfield.

name: Boston
headline: Brownstones on filled marsh, three-deckers on the hills,
and every commuter rail line running home to it.
answer: Boston is the capital of Massachusetts, a Suffolk County city of 675,647 people (2020 Census) made up of 23 neighborhoods. Its housing is mostly attached and multi-unit: brownstone and brick row houses near the center, and triple-deckers, mostly built between the 1880s and 1930s, farther out. Single-family sales are a small and unrepresentative slice of the market: The Warren Group's Boston row counted 50 in 2025 against 1,611 condo sales, and it reports neighborhoods such as Dorchester, Jamaica Plain and Charlestown on separate rows. Every MBTA commuter rail line ends at South Station or North Station, and I-93 and I-90 meet downtown.
overview: Puritan settlers founded Boston on the Shawmut Peninsula in 1630, set aside Boston Common in 1634 and opened Boston Latin School in 1635. Much of today's city is made land: the South End was built on tidal marsh beginning in 1849, and the Back Bay was filled between 1857 and about 1882, which is why their streets run in regular grids of Victorian row houses. Boston became a city in 1822 and grew by annexation, taking in Roxbury in 1868, Dorchester in 1870, Charlestown, Brighton (including present-day Allston) and West Roxbury, which included Jamaica Plain, in 1874, and Hyde Park in 1912.

The city recognizes 23 neighborhoods, from Beacon Hill and the North End to Hyde Park and West Roxbury. On Beacon Hill, Federal-style brick row houses, the first built between 1803 and 1805, climb toward Charles Bulfinch's gold-domed State House of 1798. Frederick Law Olmsted's Emerald Necklace links about 1,100 acres of parks over 7 miles, from the Back Bay Fens through Jamaica Pond and the Arnold Arboretum to Franklin Park. The Big Dig, which concluded in December 2007, moved the elevated Central Artery of I-93 into tunnels, and the Rose Kennedy Greenway opened on the vacated land in October 2008. The 2.5-mile Freedom Trail runs from downtown to the Bunker Hill Monument in Charlestown, and public ferries reach several of the Boston Harbor Islands. This is one city guide for now; neighborhood guides are planned.

Boston plans its own zoning: the state's MBTA Communities rules do not apply, because Boston is exempt from the Zoning Act, including Section 3A. A city ordinance signed in April 2024 created the Boston Planning Department, and most former Boston Planning and Development Agency staff moved into it that July. The Zoning Commission adopted six Squares + Streets districts on April 17, 2024, allowing mixed-use buildings and multifamily housing in neighborhood centers near transit; Mattapan Square was mapped first, in May 2024, Roslindale Square followed on May 22, 2025, and a December 2025 amendment added two more district types. Since October 2024, projects of seven or more units must make 20 percent of them income-restricted, up from 13 percent. In 2024 the city approved projects totaling 3,575 net new residential units, 1,210 of them income-restricted.

housing.text: Boston's triple-deckers were mostly built between the 1880s and 1930s, and the city has studied new versions of the type for neighborhoods including Roxbury, Mattapan, Dorchester and Hyde Park. Near the center, the Back Bay, South End and Charlestown are known for 19th-century brownstone and brick row houses. Condominiums dominate sales: The Warren Group counted 1,611 condo sales and 50 single-family sales on its 2025 Boston row, so the single-family median of about $3.1 million describes a very small set of homes and not the city as a whole.

villages.name: Beacon Hill
villages.line: About a sixth of a square mile between Boston Common and the Charles River Esplanade, with Federal-style brick row houses, brick sidewalks, gas lamps and the Greek Revival townhouses of Louisburg Square; a National Historic Landmark since 1962.

villages.name: Back Bay
villages.line: Former tidal flats filled between 1857 and about 1882, laid out with Victorian brownstone row houses along Commonwealth Avenue's center mall, with Copley Square at its southeast corner.

villages.name: South End
villages.line: Built on tidal marsh beside Boston Neck from 1849, with brick and brownstone row houses from 1850 to 1880 around small residential squares; often described as the largest intact Victorian row-house district in the country.

villages.name: Jamaica Plain
villages.line: Part of Roxbury, then West Roxbury, until annexed to Boston in 1874, with triple-deckers from the 1870s onward, Jamaica Pond, and four Orange Line stations under the Southwest Corridor Park.

villages.name: Charlestown
villages.line: Laid out by Thomas Graves and settled in 1629, annexed to Boston in 1874, with red-brick row houses, the Bunker Hill Monument and the Charlestown Navy Yard.

villages.name: Dorchester
villages.line: A separate town founded in 1630 and part of Boston since 1870; the city's largest neighborhood at more than 6 square miles, with many three-decker buildings and stations on the Red Line and the Fairmount Line.

rail.line: South Station (Red Line, Silver Line SL1-SL3; Fairmount, Fall River/New Bedford, Framingham/Worcester, Franklin/Foxboro, Greenbush, Kingston, Needham and Providence/Stoughton Lines)
North Station (Orange and Green Lines; Fitchburg, Haverhill, Lowell and Newburyport/Rockport Lines; Amtrak Downeaster)
Back Bay (Orange Line, commuter rail and Amtrak)

commute.text: Boston is the hub of the MBTA: the Red, Orange, Blue and Green Lines and the Mattapan Line run through the city, and commuter rail ends at South Station or North Station, with Back Bay as a through stop. Amtrak's Acela and Northeast Regional leave from South Station and Back Bay, and the Downeaster from North Station. I-93 and I-90 meet downtown in the tunnels built by the Big Dig, US 1 crosses the Tobin Bridge, and MBTA ferries link the waterfront with Charlestown, Hingham, Hull and other harbor communities.

places.name: Boston Common
places.line: Founded in 1634, with ballfields, a tot lot and the Frog Pond, which is open for skating in winter and has a spray area in summer.

places.name: Freedom Trail
places.line: A 2.5-mile path through downtown and Charlestown linking sites of Boston National Historical Park, including Faneuil Hall and the Old South Meeting House.

places.name: Charlestown Navy Yard
places.line: One of the country's first naval shipyards, home to USS Constitution and the museum ship USS Cassin Young.

places.name: Emerald Necklace
places.line: Frederick Law Olmsted's 1,100-acre chain of eight parks over 7 miles, from Charlesgate and the Back Bay Fens to Franklin Park.

places.name: Arnold Arboretum
places.line: A 281-acre preserve founded in 1872 and part of the Emerald Necklace, free and open every day.

places.name: Boston Harbor Islands
places.line: A national and state park of 34 islands and peninsulas, with public ferries to Spectacle, Georges and Peddocks Islands among others.

places.name: Rose Kennedy Greenway
places.line: A 1.5-mile park opened in October 2008 on the land freed when the Big Dig removed the elevated highway, with the Greenway Carousel.

history.text: Puritan settlers founded Boston on the Shawmut Peninsula, naming the town on September 7, 1630 (Old Style).
Boston Common was set aside, now described as the nation's first public park.
Boston was incorporated as a city on March 19, 1822.
The Tremont Street subway opened, the first subway in the United States.
The Big Dig concluded in December, having rerouted the elevated Central Artery of I-93 into the O'Neill Tunnel; the Rose Kennedy Greenway was created in the space the elevated roadway left.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Boston, MA?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, the median single-family sale price on its Boston row for calendar year 2025 was $3,092,500, across 50 sales. In 2024 it was $3,100,000, across 51 sales. That is not a citywide median, and it is a small and unrepresentative sample: the same row counted 1,611 condo sales in 2025 at a median of $945,000, and neighborhoods such as Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, Charlestown and West Roxbury are reported on separate rows.

faq.q: Why is the single-family median on Boston's Warren Group row so high?
faq.a: Boston is mostly condominiums, triple-deckers and other multi-unit buildings, so few single-family homes trade on The Warren Group's Boston row: 50 in 2025. A handful of high-priced sales can set the median. Condo sales on the same row numbered 1,611, at a median of $945,000.

faq.q: Does Boston have commuter rail?
faq.a: Yes. Every MBTA commuter rail line ends at South Station or North Station, Back Bay is a through stop, and the Fairmount Line has stations in Dorchester. The Red, Orange, Blue and Green Lines also run through the city.

faq.q: Which school district serves Boston?
faq.a: Boston Public Schools. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Boston, MA?
faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, Boston's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $12.40 per $1,000 of assessed value, and commercial, industrial and personal property pay $26.96. Boston's residential exemption for owner-occupants is 35% of the average residential assessed value in FY2026, under the City Council's classification order; the Assessing Department confirms the dollar amount.

faq.q: How is Boston changing its zoning for new housing?
faq.a: Boston is exempt from the state Zoning Act, including the MBTA Communities law, and sets its own rules. Squares + Streets districts, adopted on April 17, 2024, allow mixed-use and multifamily buildings in neighborhood centers near transit and were mapped first in Mattapan Square and then in Roslindale Square. Since October 2024, projects of seven or more units must make 20 percent of them income-restricted.

neighborhoods.name: Back Bay
headline: Brownstone rows on filled tidal flats,
laid out one alphabetical cross street at a time.
neighborhoods.answer: Back Bay is a Boston neighborhood built on tidal flats filled between 1857 and 1882, with 18,190 residents in 2020 (2020 Census, Boston Planning Department tabulation). Its housing is mostly Victorian brownstone row houses of three to five stories on Beacon, Marlborough and Commonwealth, with shops along Newbury and Boylston Streets. Back Bay station serves the Orange Line, four commuter rail lines and Amtrak, and the Green Line stops at Arlington, Copley, Hynes Convention Center and Prudential.
neighborhoods.meta: Back Bay, Boston: brownstone rows on land filled from 1857 to 1882, the Commonwealth Avenue Mall, Copley Square, and rail at Back Bay station. Sourced guide.

boundaries.text: As defined by the Neighborhood Association of the Back Bay, the Charles River to the north, Arlington Street and Park Square to the east, Columbus Avenue, Huntington Avenue, Dalton Street and the Massachusetts Turnpike to the south, and Charlesgate East to the west. The smaller Back Bay Architectural District runs from Back Street to Boylston Street between Arlington Street and Charlesgate East.

overview: Back Bay was a tidal bay of the Charles River until the 19th century. The Boston and Roxbury Mill Corporation, chartered in 1814, built a milldam across it that doubled as a toll road; the basin behind it trapped sewage and the venture failed. Filling of the area enclosed by the dam began in 1857, and construction of houses followed from 1859. By 1882 the present neighborhood had been filled, and the City of Boston credits the mid-century landfilling with more than 450 acres of usable land by the 1880s. Arthur Gilman's plan, modeled on Haussmann's Paris, set five parallel east-west streets, Beacon, Marlborough, Commonwealth, Newbury and Boylston, crossed by streets named in alphabetical order from Arlington to Hereford.

Commonwealth Avenue runs down the middle of the grid on a 32-acre mall that Gilman designed in 1856 in the French boulevard style, the green link between the Public Garden and Frederick Law Olmsted's park system. The row houses, three to five stories, were held to setbacks written into the lot deeds, so the blocks read as continuous walls. Commercial use reached Boylston Street around 1880 and Newbury Street in the early 20th century, often by adapting existing row houses. Copley Square gathers H. H. Richardson's Trinity Church (1872 to 1877) and the Boston Public Library's McKim Building (1895), and the 52-story Prudential Tower, completed in 1964, rises to the south.

The Back Bay Architectural District was established in 1966 to regulate exterior changes, and it was expanded in 1974, 1979 and 1981. All proposed exterior work goes to the Back Bay Architectural Commission, and approval is needed before work begins. The district was added to the National Register of Historic Places on August 14, 1973. Along the river, the Charles River Esplanade was built after the Charles River Dam was completed in 1910, and pedestrian overpasses connect it to the city's streets.

housing.text: Back Bay's housing is mostly Victorian brownstone row houses of three to five stories, built from 1859 as the land was filled. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2014 to 2018 American Community Survey counts 11,992 housing units, 9,842 of them occupied; 31.8% of occupied units were owner occupied and 68.2% renter occupied.

areas.name: Back Bay Architectural District
areas.line: The residential core from Back Street to Boylston Street, between Arlington Street and Charlesgate East: Beacon, Marlborough and Commonwealth crossed by the alphabetical streets, where all exterior work is reviewed by the Back Bay Architectural Commission.

areas.name: Newbury and Boylston Streets
areas.line: The shopping streets of the neighborhood; commercial development started on Boylston Street around 1880 and on Newbury Street in the early 20th century, in some cases by adapting existing row houses.

areas.name: Copley Square
areas.line: A public square in the southeast of the neighborhood, framed by Trinity Church and the Boston Public Library's Central Library.

areas.name: Prudential Center
areas.line: The mixed-use complex in the south of the neighborhood around the 52-story Prudential Tower, completed in 1964, with Prudential station on the Green Line.

rail.line: Commuter rail: Framingham/Worcester, Needham, Franklin/Foxboro and Providence/Stoughton Lines

commute.text: Back Bay station, at 145 Dartmouth Street, serves the Orange Line, the Framingham/Worcester, Needham, Franklin/Foxboro and Providence/Stoughton commuter rail lines, and Amtrak's Acela, Northeast Regional and the Boston section of the Lake Shore Limited. The Green Line stops at Arlington, Copley, Hynes Convention Center and Prudential. The Massachusetts Turnpike forms part of the neighborhood's southern boundary.

places.name: Commonwealth Avenue Mall
places.line: A 32-acre promenade designed by Arthur Gilman in 1856 in the French boulevard style, with monuments along its center and a link from the Public Garden to the Olmsted parks.

places.name: Trinity Church
places.line: H. H. Richardson's Richardsonian Romanesque church on Copley Square, built from 1872 to 1877 and designated a National Historic Landmark in 1970.

places.name: Boston Public Library, Central Library
places.line: At 700 Boylston Street on Copley Square: Charles Follen McKim's 1895 building, with the Bates Hall reading room, and Philip Johnson's 1972 Boylston Street building in the same pink Milford granite.

places.name: Charles River Esplanade
places.line: State parkland along the Charles River created with the 1910 dam and expanded between 1928 and 1936, with the Hatch Shell stage, built in 1941, near the Arthur Fiedler footbridge at Arlington Street.

places.name: Public Garden
places.line: Established in 1837 across Arlington Street as the first public botanical garden in America, with the Lagoon and the Swan Boats run by the Paget family for over 100 years.

places.name: Gibson House Museum
places.line: A Victorian house museum at 137 Beacon Street, home to three generations of the Gibson family from 1859 to 1954.

history.text: The Boston and Roxbury Mill Corporation was chartered to build a milldam across the bay that also served as a toll road.
Filling of the area enclosed by the dam began; the present neighborhood was filled by 1882.
The Back Bay Architectural District was established; it was later expanded in 1974, 1979 and 1981.
The district was added to the National Register of Historic Places on August 14, 1973.

neighborhoods.name: Beacon Hill
headline: Brick rows and cobblestone lanes
climbing from Charles Street to the State House.
neighborhoods.answer: Beacon Hill is a Boston neighborhood on the hill behind the Massachusetts State House, between Boston Common and the Charles River, with 9,336 residents in 2020 (2020 Census, Boston Planning Department tabulation). Its housing is mostly Federal and Greek Revival brick row houses built after the State House was completed in 1798, protected since 1955 as the Historic Beacon Hill District. The Red Line stops at Charles/MGH and Park Street, and the Blue Line at Bowdoin.
neighborhoods.meta: Beacon Hill, Boston: Federal and Greek Revival row houses behind the 1798 State House, Louisburg Square, Charles Street, and the Red Line at Charles/MGH.

boundaries.text: Bounded by Storrow Drive, Cambridge Street, Bowdoin Street, Park Street and Beacon Street, plus the block bounded by Beacon, Tremont and Park Streets, with the Charles River Esplanade to the west and Boston Common and the Public Garden to the south.

overview: Beacon Hill takes its name from a signal beacon set on its summit in 1634. William Blaxton built a house and orchard on the south slope in 1625, and Beacon Street was established in 1708 from a cow path to Boston Common. Development of the hill began with Charles Bulfinch's Massachusetts State House, whose cornerstone was laid on July 4, 1795, and which was completed in January 1798. In 1795, 18 1/2 or 19 acres of grassland west of the State House were bought, most of it from John Singleton Copley, and the Mount Vernon Proprietors were formed to develop the area. Between 1807 and 1832 the hill was cut down from 138 feet to 80, and the surrounding waters were filled, creating the level Flat of the Hill west of Charles Street.

Asher Benjamin, Solomon Willard and Alexander Parris designed houses on the hill in the Federal and Greek Revival styles, and apartment buildings were added later in the 19th century. Louisburg Square, surveyed in the 1820s, is lined with Greek Revival houses built between 1834 and 1847 around a fenced oval owned and kept by the Louisburg Square Proprietors, not the city. Acorn Street, a narrow cobblestone lane, was once home to coachmen employed by households on Mount Vernon and Chestnut Streets. Charles Street, at the foot of the hill, is the neighborhood's commercial spine and gives the Red Line's Charles/MGH station its name. On the North Slope, the African Meeting House, built in 1806, and the Abiel Smith School, opened in 1835, are part of the Boston African American National Historic Site.

In 1955 the state created the Historic Beacon Hill District, the first historic district in Massachusetts, starting with the South Slope; the Flat of the Hill and the North Slope were added in 1958 and 1963, and the district was expanded again in 1975 and 2024. All exterior work visible from a public way, including views from the Common, the Public Garden, Storrow Drive, the Esplanade and the Longfellow Bridge, needs approval from the Beacon Hill Architectural Commission before work starts or materials are bought. Beacon Hill was designated a National Historic Landmark District on December 19, 1962, and listed on the National Register on October 15, 1966.

housing.text: Beacon Hill's housing is Federal and Greek Revival brick row houses, apartment buildings added later in the 19th century, and former stables and carriage houses converted into lofts and studios. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2014 to 2018 American Community Survey counts 6,077 housing units, 5,325 of them occupied; 33.5% of occupied units were owner occupied and 66.5% renter occupied.

areas.name: South Slope
areas.line: The side of the hill facing Boston Common, behind the State House; the first section protected when the Historic Beacon Hill District was created in 1955.

areas.name: North Slope
areas.line: The side of the hill falling toward Cambridge Street, added to the historic district in 1963, where the African Meeting House and Abiel Smith School stand at the center of the Boston African American National Historic Site.

areas.name: Flat of the Hill
areas.line: Level land built on fill west of Charles Street, between Beacon and Cambridge Streets, added to the historic district in 1958.

areas.name: Charles Street
areas.line: The commercial spine of the neighborhood, running south from Charles Circle at the foot of the hill; it gives the Red Line's Charles/MGH station its name.

commute.text: The Red Line stops at Charles/MGH, at Cambridge and Charles Streets, and at Park Street, where it meets the Green Line; the Blue Line stops at Bowdoin. There is no commuter rail station in the neighborhood; the Red Line continues to South Station, where eight commuter rail lines end. Storrow Drive runs along the river edge.

places.name: Massachusetts State House
places.line: Charles Bulfinch's state capitol on Beacon Street across from Boston Common, completed in 1798; Paul Revere's company sheathed its dome in copper in 1802, and it was gilded in 1874.

places.name: Louisburg Square
places.line: A private oval park between Pinckney and Mount Vernon Streets, ringed by Greek Revival houses built from 1834 to 1847, with statues of Columbus and Aristides the Just at either end.

places.name: Acorn Street
places.line: A narrow cobblestone lane that was once home to coachmen employed by households on Mount Vernon and Chestnut Streets.

places.name: African Meeting House and Abiel Smith School
places.line: Cared for by the Museum of African American History on the North Slope; the meeting house was the religious, educational and political center of Boston's Black community in the 1800s, and the school opened in 1835. Park rangers lead walks on the Black Heritage Trail.

places.name: Nichols House Museum
places.line: A historic house at 55 Mount Vernon Street, open for tours, programs and events.

places.name: Boston Common
places.line: Founded in 1634 at the foot of the hill, with ballfields, a tot lot and the Frog Pond, used for skating in winter and as a spray pool in summer.

places.name: Charles River Esplanade

neighborhoods.name: South End
headline: Brick and brownstone rows around small squares,
built on the marsh around Boston Neck.
neighborhoods.answer: The South End is a Boston neighborhood built from 1849 on filled tidal marsh around Boston Neck, with 30,904 residents in 2020 (2020 Census, Boston Planning Department tabulation, which counts Bay Village with the South End). Its housing is brick and brownstone row houses built from 1850 to 1880 around residential squares such as Union Park, protected as the South End Landmark District since 1983. The Orange Line stops at Back Bay and Massachusetts Avenue, and Silver Line SL4 and SL5 buses run on Washington Street.
neighborhoods.meta: South End, Boston: Victorian brick and brownstone rows from 1850 to 1880 around Union Park and other squares, the Southwest Corridor Park and the Orange Line.

boundaries.text: The South End Historic District on the National Register is bounded by the Southwest Corridor Park to the northwest, the Massachusetts Turnpike to the north, Herald Street to the east, Albany Street to the southeast and Massachusetts Avenue to the southwest; the neighborhood borders Back Bay, Chinatown and Roxbury.

overview: The South End was tidal marsh around Boston Neck, the strip of land joining Boston to Roxbury; Washington Street follows the original causeway between them. In 1801 Charles Bulfinch proposed a single oval park there, Columbia Square, which by 1814 appeared as two halves on either side of Washington Street, today's Blackstone and Franklin Squares; the area developed slowly until the 1850s. Large-scale filling made the rest of the neighborhood, and construction began on January 7, 1849. The main period of development, from 1850 to 1873, produced brick and brownstone row houses built as single-family homes. After the Panic of 1873 many of the houses were converted to multi-unit housing, and by the turn of the century lodging houses were almost the only residential buildings being built.

The row houses, built between 1850 and 1880 in brick and brownstone, mix Greek Revival, Italianate and later Victorian styles, and the neighborhood has eleven residential parks. Union Park, an elliptical park laid out by Ellis S. Chesbrough, had its lots auctioned in June 1851 and every house finished by 1859, with bowfront and square-front bays facing a cast-iron fence copied from Louisburg Square. Chester Square, laid out in 1850 as a larger oval, became part of Massachusetts Avenue in 1891. The Cyclorama, built in 1884 to show a panoramic painting of the Battle of Gettysburg, is now part of the Boston Center for the Arts, and Patrick Keely's Gothic Revival Cathedral of the Holy Cross, at 1400 Washington Street, was dedicated in 1875.

The South End Landmark District, designated in 1983, requires South End Landmark District Commission approval for exterior work on front facades, rooftops and some side and rear elevations before it begins. The National Register district was listed on May 8, 1973, with boundary increases in 2014 and 2025. Along the northwest edge, the Southwest Corridor Park, managed by the state Department of Conservation and Recreation, opened in segments from 1987 and was completed in 1990 over and beside the Orange Line and the rail corridor, with paths, courts and playgrounds. East of Washington Street, the area known as SoWa (South of Washington) runs roughly from Albany to Washington Street between East Berkeley Street and Massachusetts Avenue.

housing.text: The South End's row houses were built as single-family brick and brownstone homes between 1850 and 1880, and many were converted to multi-unit housing after the Panic of 1873. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2014 to 2018 American Community Survey counts 17,936 housing units, 16,606 of them occupied; 38.6% of occupied units were owner occupied and 61.4% renter occupied.
