neighborhoods.name: Charlestown
headline: Red-brick rows on Breed's Hill,
and a navy yard turned to new uses on the harbor.
neighborhoods.answer: Charlestown is Boston's oldest neighborhood, founded in 1629 on a peninsula between the Charles and Mystic Rivers and annexed to Boston in 1874, with 19,120 residents in 2020 (2020 Census, Boston Planning Department tabulation). Its housing is largely red-brick row houses on Bunker Hill and Breed's Hill, plus buildings of the former Navy Yard converted to residential and other uses. The Orange Line stops at Community College and Sullivan Square, and the MBTA's Charlestown Ferry runs from the Navy Yard to Long Wharf.
neighborhoods.meta: Charlestown, Boston: founded 1629, red-brick rows on Breed's Hill, the Bunker Hill Monument and Navy Yard, Orange Line and ferry. 2025 Warren Group prices.

boundaries.text: A peninsula north of the Charles River, opposite downtown Boston, bordered by the Mystic River and Boston Harbor, with I-93 along its western edge, the Navy Yard on the harbor, and Sullivan Square where the Charlestown Neck once joined it to the mainland.

overview: Charlestown was laid out by Thomas Graves and settled in 1629, and the City of Boston calls it the city's oldest neighborhood; John Winthrop's company stopped here in 1630 before crossing the Charles River to found Boston. On June 17, 1775, the Battle of Bunker Hill was fought on Breed's Hill, and British forces burned almost the whole town. The first bridge to Boston opened in 1786, and the Navy Yard opened in 1800. Charlestown voters approved annexation on October 7, 1873, by 2,240 to 1,947, and it became part of Boston on January 5, 1874.

The peninsula rises to two small hills, Bunker Hill to the north and Breed's Hill, both covered mostly in housing, much of it red-brick row houses. The 221-foot granite Bunker Hill Monument, reached by 294 steps, was dedicated on Breed's Hill in 1843. City Square, in the southern part of the neighborhood, was the site of the city hall before annexation, and Sullivan Square sits where landfill erased the narrow Charlestown Neck. The Navy Yard closed on July 1, 1974; the National Park Service holds 25 acres as part of Boston National Historical Park, and most of the redeveloped buildings were converted to office, commercial and residential use. The Orange Line has run through Charlestown since April 7, 1975, when Community College and Sullivan Square stations replaced the City Square and Thompson Square stations of the Charlestown Elevated, which had opened in 1901.

Two large changes are under way. The Bunker Hill Housing redevelopment, a partnership of the Boston Housing Authority, the Joseph J. Corcoran Company, Leggat McCall and the Charlestown Resident Alliance, is replacing 1,100 public housing units with 2,699 public, income-restricted and market-rate rental units, with 73,000 square feet of retail and civic space; its first building broke ground in June 2023, and the next, a nine-story building of 265 units, was expected to start in mid to late 2025. On September 28, 2023, after four years of work, the Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted PLAN: Charlestown, which sets out how new growth can fit along the Rutherford Avenue corridor and in Sullivan Square and proposes new zoning to allow more housing and retail in existing industrial areas.

housing.text: Charlestown's housing stock is largely red-brick row houses, many near the waterfront, along with homes in converted Navy Yard buildings and the Bunker Hill public housing now being rebuilt. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2014 to 2018 American Community Survey counts 9,536 housing units, 9,050 of them occupied; 46.1% of occupied units were owner occupied and 53.9% renter occupied.

areas.name: Charlestown Navy Yard
areas.line: The former naval shipyard on the harbor, open from 1800 to 1974; 25 acres are part of Boston National Historical Park and most of the rest has been redeveloped for office, commercial and residential use.

areas.name: Monument Square and Breed's Hill
areas.line: The hilltop around the Bunker Hill Monument, whose museum stands at 43 Monument Square.

areas.name: City Square
areas.line: In the southern part of the neighborhood, the site of the city hall before annexation; US 1 passes below City Square and Paul Revere Park.

areas.name: Sullivan Square
areas.line: Where the Charlestown Neck once met the mainland, with an Orange Line station and busway; one of the focus areas of PLAN: Charlestown, adopted by the Boston Planning & Development Agency board on September 28, 2023.

commute.text: The Orange Line stops at Community College, on Austin Street beneath the I-93 viaduct, and at Sullivan Square, which has a busway; routes 92 and 93 run from Sullivan Square to downtown. The MBTA's Charlestown Ferry links the Navy Yard with Long Wharf. Charlestown has no commuter rail station. I-93 and US 1, by way of the Tobin Bridge, pass through.

places.name: Bunker Hill Monument
places.line: A 221-foot granite obelisk on Breed's Hill marking the battle of June 17, 1775, dedicated in 1843 and climbed by a spiral stair of 294 steps.

places.name: USS Constitution
places.line: Launched in 1797 and known as Old Ironsides, the world's oldest commissioned warship still afloat, usually berthed at Pier 1 of the Navy Yard and open to visitors year round with free tours.

places.name: USS Cassin Young
places.line: A Fletcher-class destroyer that served from 1943 to 1960, berthed at the Navy Yard, which the National Park Service stewards in partnership with the U.S. Navy and the USS Constitution Museum; the Navy Yard grounds are open 24 hours a day.

places.name: Paul Revere Park
places.line: A five-acre park along the Charles River between the Freedom Trail and the Zakim Bunker Hill Bridge, built as Big Dig mitigation and first opened in 1999.

places.name: Phipps Street Burying Ground
places.line: A 1.8-acre burial ground created in 1630, where John Harvard is buried; listed on the National Register in 1974.

places.name: Winthrop Square (Training Field)
places.line: A historic park and former militia training field, home to the Charlestown Civil War Memorial.

history.text: Thomas Graves laid out Charlestown, settled that year.
The Battle of Bunker Hill was fought on June 17, and British forces burned almost all of the town.
Charlestown was annexed to Boston on January 5, 1874, after voters approved it 2,240 to 1,947.

neighborhoods.name: Jamaica Plain
headline: A kettle pond, an arboretum and a cemetery park,
with the Orange Line running under a linear park.
neighborhoods.answer: Jamaica Plain is a Boston neighborhood of 4.4 square miles between Jamaica Pond and Franklin Park, part of the town of West Roxbury until it was annexed to Boston in 1874. Its housing runs from triple-deckers built from the 1870s onward to Victorian houses on former estates such as Sumner Hill. The Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 41,012 people there in 2020. Four Orange Line stations run under the Southwest Corridor Park, and the Needham Line stops at Forest Hills.
neighborhoods.meta: Jamaica Plain, Boston: triple-deckers and Victorian houses between Jamaica Pond and Franklin Park, with four Orange Line stops and the Needham Line.

boundaries.text: Jamaica Plain, originally part of Roxbury, meets Roxbury at Egleston Square. Its sections run from Pondside, by Jamaica Pond and the Jamaicaway, and Parkside, beside Franklin Park, south to Forest Hills, near the Arnold Arboretum and Forest Hills Cemetery.

overview: Settlement south of Parker Hill began shortly after 1630, when Boston and Roxbury were founded, and the name Jamaica first appears on maps in the late 1650s. In 1676 John Ruggles and Hugh Thomas gave land for the community's first school, later the Eliot School. From 1795 to 1886, the Jamaica Pond Aqueduct Corporation supplied water from the pond to Boston, Roxbury and later West Roxbury. The Boston and Providence Rail Road arrived in 1834, and in 1851 estate owners here helped split from Roxbury to form the town of West Roxbury, which voted to join Boston in 1873; annexation took effect in 1874. Breweries opened too: Highland Spring on Heath Street from 1867 and Haffenreffer, near Boylston and Amory Streets, from 1871 until 1964.

Triple-deckers first appeared in the 1870s and spread quickly in the 1890s. Larger houses went up on former estates: Sumner Hill on the Greenough land, Parley Vale and Robinwood Avenue in the 1880s, and Moss Hill and Woodland Road on Bowditch family land in the 1890s. By the early 20th century most buildable lots were filled. Much of the neighborhood's edge is parkland in Frederick Law Olmsted's Emerald Necklace: Olmsted Park and Jamaica Pond along the Jamaicaway, the Arnold Arboretum and the Arborway in the south, and Franklin Park beside the Parkside section; the 1848 Forest Hills Cemetery is in the Forest Hills section.

In 1969 Governor Francis Sargent cancelled a planned extension of I-95 through the area after community opposition. The cleared land became the Southwest Corridor: the Orange Line moved from the elevated Washington Street line into a below-grade cut in May 1987, and the park above it was completed in 1990. On March 2, 2017, the Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted PLAN: JP/ROX, guidelines for about 250 acres between Forest Hills, Egleston Square and Jackson Square, generally bounded by Washington Street, Columbus Avenue and Amory Street, covering housing, jobs, urban design and transportation.

housing.text: Jamaica Plain's housing mixes wood-frame triple-deckers, built from the 1870s and especially in the 1890s, with late-19th-century single-family houses on former estates such as Sumner Hill and Moss Hill. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 18,129 occupied housing units in the neighborhood, 45.6% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: The Monument and Centre Street
areas.line: The area around the intersection of Centre and South Streets, named for the Soldiers' Monument there; the 1760 Loring-Greenough House stands on Monument Square at 12 South Street.

areas.name: Hyde Square
areas.line: The area around Centre, Day and Perkins Streets, extending east along Centre Street toward Roxbury.

areas.name: Jackson Square and Egleston Square
areas.line: Squares at the northern edge, on Columbus Avenue and Washington Street at the Roxbury line; Jackson Square has an Orange Line station, and both fall within the PLAN: JP/ROX study area.

areas.name: Forest Hills
areas.line: The section roughly bounded by the Arborway, Morton Street, Walk Hill Street, South Street and Forest Hills Cemetery, with Forest Hills station at Washington Street and Hyde Park Avenue, rebuilt in 1987 for the Orange Line and commuter rail.

commute.text: The Orange Line runs below street level through Jamaica Plain to Back Bay and downtown, and Forest Hills station, at Washington Street and Hyde Park Avenue, is also a Needham Line commuter rail stop and the terminal for 16 MBTA bus routes. The Green Line E branch ends at Heath Street, and the 39 bus is the neighborhood's main bus route. The Southwest Corridor Park carries a bike path beside the Orange Line, and the Jamaicaway and Arborway run along the Emerald Necklace.

places.name: Jamaica Pond
places.line: A spring-fed glacial kettle hole more than 50 feet deep, taken into the park system in 1891, with a boathouse and bandstand from 1912 and boat rentals in summer.

places.name: Arnold Arboretum
places.line: A 281-acre preserve founded in 1872 and part of the Emerald Necklace, open free every day.

places.name: Franklin Park
places.line: Olmsted's 485-acre park, Boston's largest open space, with the Franklin Park Zoo, White Stadium and the William J. Devine Golf Course; it connects Jamaica Plain with Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan and Roslindale.

places.name: Forest Hills Cemetery
places.line: A garden cemetery founded in 1848 as Roxbury's municipal cemetery and designed by Henry A. S. Dearborn, entered from Morton Street; it was added to the National Register in 2004.

places.name: Loring-Greenough House
places.line: A 1760 country house at 12 South Street, owned since 1924 by the Jamaica Plain Tuesday Club and designated a Boston Landmark in 1999.

places.name: Southwest Corridor Park
places.line: A linear park managed by DCR from Back Bay station to Forest Hills, built over the Orange Line on land cleared for a cancelled highway; its first segments opened in 1987.

places.name: Haffenreffer Brewery buildings
places.line: The former Haffenreffer brewery near Boylston and Amory Streets, which brewed from 1871 until 1964; the old buildings now house the Boston Beer Company, brewer of Samuel Adams.

history.text: John Ruggles and Hugh Thomas donated land for the community's first school, later named the Eliot School.
Jamaica Plain became part of the new town of West Roxbury, set off from Roxbury.
Annexation to Boston took effect after West Roxbury voters approved it in 1873.
The rebuilt Forest Hills station opened on May 4, and Orange Line trains began running through the Southwest Corridor on May 7, replacing the elevated line on Washington Street.

neighborhoods.name: South Boston
headline: Dorchester Heights at the center,
Castle Island and three miles of beach and parkland at the end of Broadway.
neighborhoods.answer: South Boston is a Boston neighborhood on the former Dorchester Neck, south and east of Fort Point Channel along Dorchester Bay, annexed to Boston in 1804. Its housing includes 19th-century brick and mansard row houses and flat-roofed triple-deckers, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 37,917 people there in 2020, with the South Boston Waterfront counted separately. The Red Line stops at Broadway and Andrew, and Castle Island anchors three miles of shoreline parks.
neighborhoods.meta: South Boston: row houses and triple-deckers from Dorchester Heights to Castle Island, with Red Line stops at Broadway and Andrew and three miles of shoreline parks.

boundaries.text: South Boston lies south and east of Fort Point Channel, along Dorchester Bay, with Castle Island beside City Point and Andrew station on its west side. The Seaport, or South Boston Waterfront, north of the residential streets is treated by the city's planners as a separate neighborhood.

overview: South Boston was Dorchester Neck, a narrow peninsula belonging to the town of Dorchester. On the night of March 4, 1776, Continental troops fortified Dorchester Heights, and the British evacuated Boston on March 17. Boston annexed the peninsula in 1804, bridges over Fort Point Channel tied it to downtown, and landfill widened its connection to the mainland. In 1822 land on the peninsula was set aside for public institutions, including a jail and an almshouse; after they moved, East Broadway was extended to the end of the peninsula in 1854 and 4.5 acres became Independence Square.

The streets climb to Dorchester Heights, the highest area of South Boston. Near the top of Telegraph Hill, an 1849 reservoir was later filled and replaced by South Boston High School in 1901, and the rest of the summit was laid out in the 1850s as Thomas Park, now centered on a 115-foot marble monument completed in 1902. Mansard and brick row houses, some with marble and sandstone fronts, went up around Independence Square in the fifteen years after the Civil War. At City Point the granite Fort Independence, built between 1833 and 1848, stands on Castle Island, which the city joined to the mainland by filling the flats between 1890 and the 1920s; Day Boulevard now runs past Pleasure Bay, M Street Beach and Carson Beach.

Recent city planning has looked at the neighborhood's edges. The Boston Planning & Development Agency completed PLAN: South Boston Dorchester Avenue in December 2016, with the projects reviewed under it mostly on Dorchester Avenue, Old Colony Avenue and nearby streets, and a follow-up transportation plan was finalized in 2021. To the north, the waterfront along Fort Point Channel and Boston Harbor was the focus of the city's 1,000-acre Innovation District plan announced in 2010, and the city's research tables report it as the separate South Boston Waterfront neighborhood.

housing.text: South Boston's housing includes mansard and brick row houses from the 1860s and 1870s around Independence Square and along East Broadway, and triple-deckers, which here were mostly built with flat roofs. The Boston Housing Authority's Mary Ellen McCormack (1936) and Old Colony (1941) developments are in the neighborhood, and the second phase of Old Colony's redevelopment was completed in 2014. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 17,109 occupied housing units, 43.4% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: City Point
areas.line: The eastern end of the peninsula near Castle Island, reached by East Broadway and Day Boulevard, where MBTA bus routes 7, 9, 10 and 11 end at the City Point bus terminal.

areas.name: Independence Square
areas.line: A 4.5-acre square on East Broadway laid out in 1854, ringed by mansard and brick row houses built mostly in the fifteen years after the Civil War, including the Harrison Loring House at 789 East Broadway, the first house on the square.

areas.name: Dorchester Heights and Telegraph Hill
areas.line: The highest area of South Boston, with Thomas Park and the Dorchester Heights Monument on the summit of Telegraph Hill and South Boston High School on the site of an 1849 reservoir; a 40-acre area centered on Thomas Park was listed on the National Register as the Dorchester Heights Historic District in 2001.

areas.name: West Broadway and Andrew Square
areas.line: The western side along Broadway and Dorchester Avenue, served by the Broadway and Andrew Red Line stations; Andrew Square is where Dorchester Avenue, Dorchester Street, Southampton Street and Boston Street meet.

commute.text: The Red Line's Broadway station, at Dorchester Avenue and Broadway, opened in 1917, and Andrew station, at Andrew Square, in 1918; both run north to South Station, where the Fairmount, Needham, Providence/Stoughton and other south-side commuter rail lines end. MBTA bus routes 7, 9, 10 and 11 cross the neighborhood to the City Point terminal, and Andrew connects with routes including the 10, 16, 17, 18 and 171. The Silver Line serves the separate Waterfront area, and the Big Dig put I-93 below ground.

places.name: Castle Island and Fort Independence
places.line: A DCR park at 2010 Day Boulevard, where the Castle Island Loop circles the granite Fort Independence, built from 1833 and listed on the National Register in 1970; open sunrise to sunset.

places.name: Pleasure Bay, M Street Beach and Carson Beach
places.line: Part of a three-mile stretch of beach and parkland along Day Boulevard, with an accessible loop around Pleasure Bay; dogs are not allowed on the beach from May 1 through September 15.

places.name: Dorchester Heights Monument
places.line: A white marble Georgian Revival tower by Peabody and Stearns, completed in 1902 to mark the fortification of March 4, 1776, and stewarded by the National Park Service as part of Boston National Historical Park.

places.name: Thomas Park
places.line: A roughly elliptical park of walks and ornamental plantings laid out in the 1850s on the summit of Telegraph Hill on Dorchester Heights, centered on the monument.

places.name: Independence Square
places.line: A 4.5-acre park created in 1854 on East Broadway, which received 150 trees and granite steps in 1874.

places.name: Saint Augustine Chapel
places.line: A chapel completed in 1819 and described as the oldest Catholic church in Massachusetts.

history.text: Continental troops fortified Dorchester Heights on March 4, and the British evacuated Boston on March 17.
Boston annexed South Boston, part of the town of Dorchester's Dorchester Neck.
Work began on the present granite Fort Independence on Castle Island, substantially complete by 1848.
Broadway station opened on December 15 as part of the Red Line's Dorchester Extension; Andrew followed in 1918.

neighborhoods.name: West Roxbury
headline: Centre Street, three Needham Line stops,
and Bellevue Hill, the city's highest natural point.
neighborhoods.answer: West Roxbury is Boston's southwestern neighborhood, bordering Brookline, Newton, Needham and Dedham, set off from Roxbury as its own town in 1851 and annexed to Boston in 1874. Its housing is mostly single-family homes with some two-family houses, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 31,561 people there in 2020. Three Needham Line stations, Bellevue, Highland and West Roxbury, run to South Station, and Centre Street is the main business district.
neighborhoods.meta: West Roxbury, Boston: mostly single-family homes along Centre Street, three Needham Line stations, Millennium Park and Bellevue Hill, the city's highest point.

boundaries.text: West Roxbury is the southwest corner of Boston: Roslindale and Jamaica Plain lie to the northeast, Chestnut Hill and Brookline to the north, Newton to the northwest, Dedham and Needham to the southwest, and Hyde Park to the southeast; VFW Parkway runs along its western side.

overview: West Roxbury was settled in 1630 as farmland, part of the town of Roxbury, and the Westerly Burying Ground on Centre Street dates to 1683. In 1841 George and Sophia Ripley founded Brook Farm, a transcendentalist community, at the Ellis Farm on what is now Baker Street; Nathaniel Hawthorne's stay there became The Blithedale Romance. The Boston and Providence Railroad opened its West Roxbury Branch from Forest Hills to Dedham in 1849, and on May 24, 1851, West Roxbury, then including Jamaica Plain, was incorporated as a separate town. It became part of Boston on January 5, 1874.

Centre Street is the spine of the neighborhood and its business district, with the Theodore Parker Church, a Boston Landmark whose present building dates from 1900, and the Westerly Burying Ground along it. Bellevue Hill, bounded roughly by LaGrange Street, Centre Street and the West Roxbury Parkway, rises to 330 feet, the highest natural point in Boston and Suffolk County, and carries the Bellevue Standpipe. In 1906 the New Haven Railroad extended the branch from West Roxbury to Needham Junction, the route of today's Needham Line.

Open land frames the streets. Boston's 2008-2014 Open Space Plan counted 645 acres of protected open space in West Roxbury, among them the 105-acre Millennium Park, built on the former Gardner Street landfill with material excavated for the Big Dig and opened on December 7, 2000, and Allandale Woods, which the plan called the city's largest urban wild. The 616-acre Stony Brook Reservation runs south from Washington Street in West Roxbury into Hyde Park, and Brook Farm, where the state bought 148 acres of the original land in 1988, is operated by DCR as a historic site.

housing.text: West Roxbury is mostly single-family homes, with some two-family houses. Boston's 2008-2014 Open Space Plan put single-family homes at about 55% of year-round housing units and noted that over three-quarters of units were built after 1920. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 13,868 occupied housing units, 61.7% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Centre Street
areas.line: The main commercial street and business district, running the length of the neighborhood past the Theodore Parker Church and the Westerly Burying Ground.

areas.name: Bellevue Hill
areas.line: Streets on the city's highest natural point, at 330 feet, bounded roughly by LaGrange Street, Centre Street and the West Roxbury Parkway, with the Bellevue Standpipe on the summit.

areas.name: The Charles River edge
areas.line: The western side along VFW Parkway, with Millennium Park and its canoe launch on the Charles River, Brook Farm on Baker Street, and a VA hospital near the Dedham line.

commute.text: The Needham Line stops at Bellevue, Highland and West Roxbury, at 450 LaGrange Street, and runs through Roslindale Village, Forest Hills, Ruggles and Back Bay to South Station. Forest Hills, at the Jamaica Plain end of the line, connects with the Orange Line. Several MBTA bus routes run through or end in the neighborhood, and VFW Parkway and the West Roxbury Parkway are its main parkways.

places.name: Millennium Park
places.line: A park on the former Gardner Street landfill, reclaimed with material excavated for the Big Dig and opened in 2000; the city's open space plan lists 105 acres, with 21 acres of playing fields and a canoe launch on the Charles River.

places.name: Stony Brook Reservation
places.line: A 616-acre DCR reservation, one of the five original reservations of the Metropolitan Park Commission, running south from Washington Street in West Roxbury to Mother Brook in Hyde Park, with hiking and biking trails and fishing at Turtle Pond.

places.name: Brook Farm
places.line: Site of the 1841 to 1847 transcendentalist community at 670 Baker Street, a National Historic Landmark since 1965, operated by DCR as a historic site.

places.name: Westerly Burying Ground
places.line: A burying ground on Centre Street, at LaGrange Street, dating to 1683, Boston's seventh-oldest cemetery, listed on the National Register in 1987.

places.name: Theodore Parker Church
places.line: A Boston Landmark on Centre Street, its 1900 building designed by Henry Seaver, with seven Tiffany Studios windows; the original 1890 church by Alexander Wadsworth Longfellow Jr. is now the parish hall.

places.name: Allandale Woods
places.line: A wooded city urban wild at the neighborhood's northern edge, described in Boston's open space plan as the city's largest.

history.text: The Westerly Burying Ground was established, when West Roxbury was still part of Roxbury.
George and Sophia Ripley founded the Brook Farm community at the Ellis Farm; it had closed by 1847.
West Roxbury was incorporated as a town on May 24, separate from Roxbury.
West Roxbury became part of Boston on January 5.

neighborhoods.name: Dorchester
headline: Squares strung along the Red Line,
three-deckers between them, the Neponset at the edge.
neighborhoods.answer: Dorchester is Boston's largest neighborhood, more than 6 square miles between South Boston and the Neponset River, founded as a separate town in 1630 and annexed to Boston in stages that ended in 1870. Its housing mixes single-family, two-family and three-decker homes and condominiums, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 122,191 people there in 2020. Five Red Line stations, the Mattapan Line and Fairmount Line commuter rail stations including Uphams Corner, Four Corners/Geneva and Talbot Avenue serve it.
neighborhoods.meta: Dorchester, Boston: three-deckers and Victorian houses around Fields Corner, Savin Hill, Codman Square and Lower Mills, on the Red Line and Fairmount Line.

boundaries.text: Dorchester is bordered by South Boston, the South End, Roxbury, Jamaica Plain and Hyde Park; the Neponset River separates it from Quincy and Milton, and Dorchester Bay lies to the east. It is often divided into North Dorchester, the part north of Quincy, East and Freeport Streets, and South Dorchester.

overview: Settlers who came on the Mary and John landed at Columbia Point in June 1630 and founded Dorchester months before Boston. The town held what is described as the first town meeting in what became the United States on October 8, 1633, buried its dead in the North Burying Ground at today's Uphams Corner from 1634, and opened the Mather School in 1639. Israel Stoughton built a grist mill on the Neponset River in 1634, and from 1765 chocolate was refined at Lower Mills, where the Walter Baker company made it until 1965. Boston took Dorchester in pieces, starting with Dorchester Neck (now South Boston) in 1804, and annexed the rest of the town in 1870.

Dorchester grew as a streetcar suburb. The Old Colony Railroad crossed it from 1845, Dorchester Avenue carried a horse-drawn streetcar, and by 1890 the streetcar and the three-decker had come together here, with three-deckers filling the land between the old village centers. Those centers are still the neighborhood's commercial squares: Uphams Corner and Bowdoin/Geneva in the north; Fields Corner, Codman Square, Peabody Square at Ashmont, Adams Village and Lower Mills to the south. The Red Line's Dorchester stations opened in 1927 and 1928, from Columbia (now JFK/UMass) through Savin Hill, Fields Corner and Shawmut to Ashmont.

Columbia Point, where the first settlers landed, now holds UMass Boston, which moved there in 1974, the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library, dedicated in 1979, the Edward M. Kennedy Institute and the Massachusetts Archives. The Fairmount Line gained new Dorchester stations at Talbot Avenue in November 2012 and Four Corners/Geneva in July 2013, and Pope John Paul II Park opened in 2001 on a former drive-in and dump along the Neponset. In May 2024 the Boston Planning Department began a Squares + Streets plan for Fields Corner, part of a citywide program covering housing, public space, small businesses and transportation in neighborhood centers; the department's project page showed it still in progress, with no adoption date.

housing.text: Dorchester's housing includes single-family, two-family and three-family houses and condominiums. Three-decker apartment buildings went up in large numbers alongside the streetcar lines from around 1890, and Victorian houses fill hills such as Savin Hill, where lots were sold after the Civil War. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 44,979 occupied housing units, 37.3% of them owner-occupied, compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Savin Hill
areas.line: A hill above Dorchester Bay, first called Rock Hill and renamed in 1819, built up with Victorian houses after the Civil War; it has a Red Line station from 1927 and Savin Hill and Malibu beaches nearby.

areas.name: Fields Corner
areas.line: A commercial district centered on the X-shaped crossing of Dorchester Avenue and Adams Street, named for Zechariah Field, with the 1874 Fields Corner Municipal Building and a Red Line station; side streets hold three-deckers and Victorian houses.

areas.name: Ashmont
areas.line: The area around Ashmont station at Dorchester Avenue and Ashmont Street, the Red Line's southern terminus on this branch and the transfer point to the Mattapan Line, with Peabody Square's shops beside it.

areas.name: Lower Mills
areas.line: The old mill village on the Neponset River at the Milton line, where the Walter Baker chocolate buildings, a major part of them built from 1868, now hold mixed industrial, retail and residential uses; the district was listed on the National Register in 1980.

areas.name: Uphams Corner
areas.line: The square where Columbia Road meets Dudley and Stoughton Streets, named for grocer Amos Upham, with the 1918 Strand Theatre, the 1634 North Burying Ground and a Fairmount Line station.

areas.name: Codman Square
areas.line: The crossing of Washington Street and Talbot Avenue, a National Register district since 1983 that includes the 1806 Second Church in Dorchester and the 1904 Codman Square branch library; Talbot Avenue station on the Fairmount Line is nearby.

commute.text: The Red Line's Ashmont branch has five stations in Dorchester, and at Ashmont it meets the Mattapan Line trolley, which stops at Cedar Grove in southern Dorchester. The Fairmount Line runs from South Station through Newmarket, Uphams Corner, Four Corners/Geneva and Talbot Avenue toward Readville. I-93, Route 203 and Route 28 (Blue Hill Avenue) cross the neighborhood, along with Gallivan Boulevard and Morton Street.

places.name: John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum
places.line: I. M. Pei's library on a 9.5-acre site at the tip of Columbia Point, beside UMass Boston, dedicated on October 20, 1979, with a glass and steel pavilion 115 feet high.

places.name: James Blake House
places.line: Built in 1661, a date confirmed by tree-ring dating in 2007, and described as the oldest surviving house in Boston; it stands at 735 Columbia Road in Edward Everett Square and is owned by the Dorchester Historical Society.

places.name: Pope John Paul II Park
places.line: A 66-acre DCR park on the Neponset River, opened in 2001 on the site of the Neponset Drive-In and the Hallet Street dump, with trails including the Lower Neponset River Trail.

places.name: Franklin Park
places.line: Olmsted's 485-acre park, Boston's largest open space, which connects Dorchester with Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan and Roslindale; it holds the Franklin Park Zoo and the William Devine Golf Course.

places.name: Strand Theatre
places.line: A theater at Uphams Corner, opened in 1918 as one of the first built specifically for motion pictures.

places.name: Dorchester North Burying Ground
places.line: A burying ground at Uphams Corner dating to 1634, one of the oldest in the country.

places.name: Dorchester-Milton Lower Mills Industrial District
places.line: The Walter Baker chocolate complex on both banks of the Neponset, where chocolate was made from 1765 until 1965, now in mixed industrial, retail and residential use.

history.text: Settlers from the Mary and John landed at Columbia Point on June 17 and founded the town of Dorchester.
Dorchester held what is described as the first town meeting in what became the United States, on October 8.
Dr. James Baker and John Hannan began making chocolate at Lower Mills, the start of the Walter Baker company.
After a June 1869 vote, the rest of the town of Dorchester was annexed to Boston.

name: Cambridge
headline: Newtowne of 1630 on the Charles,
five Red Line stops and a reservoir to the west.
answer: Cambridge is a Middlesex County city of 118,403 people (2020 Census) on the north bank of the Charles River, across from Boston. Single-family homes are a small share of its housing: 6.4% of units, against 34.1% in buildings of more than 100 units, by the city's own count. The Warren Group recorded 105 single-family sales in 2025, a small market for a city of this size. Five Red Line stations run through Cambridge, from Alewife to Kendall/MIT, and Porter also has commuter rail.
overview: Cambridge was founded in December 1630 as Newtowne and renamed in May 1638 after the English university town, two years after the college that became Harvard was founded. George Washington took command of the Continental Army on Cambridge Common in 1775 and used the house at 105 Brattle Street as his first long-term headquarters during the siege of Boston. The West Boston Bridge of 1792 tied the town directly to Boston, and new bridges and roads turned estates and marshland into industrial and residential districts; the New England Glass Company, founded in 1818, with plants in what are now Kendall Square and East Cambridge, was the city's largest employer for much of the 19th century. Cambridge became a city in 1846. MIT moved here from Boston in 1916.

The city recognizes 13 neighborhoods on about 6.4 square miles of land. Squares strung along Massachusetts Avenue anchor them: Harvard Square beside the 22.4-acre Harvard Yard, where Massachusetts Hall has stood since 1720, Central Square with City Hall, and Porter Square farther north, while Kendall Square grew from salt marsh and 19th-century industry into an office and laboratory district beside MIT. Cambridgeport keeps streets of triple-deckers near the river. In the west, Fresh Pond Reservation surrounds the city's drinking-water reservoir, and Mount Auburn Cemetery, founded in 1831, straddles the line with Watertown. Danehy Park, a 50-acre former city dump in North Cambridge, opened as parkland in 1990.

On February 10, 2025, the City Council voted to allow multifamily housing citywide. Multifamily housing is now allowed in every zoning district except Open Space, and in the new base district, Residence C-1, residential buildings may rise to four stories (45 feet), or to six stories (74 feet) on lots of at least 5,000 square feet when 20 percent of the housing is income-restricted. Existing single-family homes may remain and new ones may still be built, and the city's inclusionary housing program continues. Since October 2020, the 100 Percent Affordable Housing Overlay, amended in 2023 and 2025, has allowed permanently affordable buildings denser than base zoning; completed projects include 52 New Street (106 rental units) and 116 Norfolk Street (62). The state lists Cambridge as compliant with the MBTA Communities law.

housing.text: By the city's inventory as of June 30, 2025, 6.4% of Cambridge's housing units are single-family homes, 11.9% are in two-unit buildings and 10.5% in three-unit buildings, while 34.1% are in buildings of more than 100 units. About two-thirds of occupied units (66.5%) are renter-occupied and 33.5% owner-occupied (2020 to 2024 American Community Survey). With so few single-family homes, The Warren Group's 105 single-family sales in 2025 reflect only a narrow part of the market.

villages.name: Harvard Square
villages.line: A triangular plaza where Massachusetts Avenue, Brattle Street and John F. Kennedy Street meet beside Harvard Yard, served by Harvard station on the Red Line and a bus hub.

villages.name: Central Square
villages.line: The seat of city government, centered where Massachusetts Avenue, Prospect Street and Western Avenue meet; a state-designated Cultural District since 2012, with Central station on the Red Line.

villages.name: Kendall Square
villages.line: Former Charles River salt marsh and industrial district where Main Street meets Broadway, named for the Kendall Boiler and Tank Company, now an office and lab district beside MIT with the Kendall/MIT Red Line stop.

villages.name: Cambridgeport
villages.line: A mostly residential neighborhood of triple-deckers between Massachusetts Avenue and the Charles River, with Magazine Beach and Fort Washington Park.

villages.name: East Cambridge
villages.line: The old Lechmere Point, once home to glassworks and factory cottages, between the Charles River, Somerville and Broadway, with Lechmere station relocated in 2022 for the Green Line Extension.

villages.name: Porter Square
villages.line: The square where Massachusetts Avenue meets Somerville Avenue, spanning Cambridge and Somerville, renamed in 1896 for Porter's Hotel and once lined with cattle yards; the Red Line reached Porter station in 1984, and it is also a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop.

commute.text: Five Red Line stations serve Cambridge, from Alewife, which has a 2,471-space MBTA garage, through Porter, Harvard and Central to Kendall/MIT. Porter is also a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop, about 15 minutes from Boston's North Station, and Lechmere in East Cambridge is on the Green Line. Route 2 enters at Alewife and runs with US 3 and Route 16 along Alewife Brook and Fresh Pond Parkways, then with US 3 along Memorial Drive beside the Charles.

places.name: Fresh Pond Reservation
places.line: 162 acres of open space around the 155-acre Fresh Pond reservoir, part of the city's drinking-water system, with nature walks and ranger programs.

places.name: Mount Auburn Cemetery
places.line: Established in 1831 between Cambridge and Watertown, a National Historic Landmark open to the public at no cost every day of the year.

places.name: Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters
places.line: A National Historic Site at 105 Brattle Street, Washington's headquarters during the siege of Boston and later Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's home, with seasonal tours and a formal garden.

places.name: Cambridge Common
places.line: Public parkland where Washington took command of the Continental Army in 1775.

places.name: Harvard Yard
places.line: A 22.4-acre grassy enclosure bounded principally by Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge Street, Broadway and Quincy Street, with Massachusetts Hall (1720), Harvard's oldest building, and Widener Library.

places.name: Danehy Park
places.line: A 50-acre North Cambridge park on a former brickyard and city dump, opened in 1990, with athletic fields, paths, a wetland area and the city's first Miyawaki forest, planted in 2021; the eastern entrance is at 99 Sherman Street.

places.name: MIT Museum
places.line: MIT's museum, founded in 1971, reopened on October 2, 2022 in the Gambrill Center at 314 Main Street in Kendall Square, beside the Kendall/MIT station; its collections include holography, robotics, architecture and the history of MIT.

places.name: Cambridge Public Library
places.line: The main library at 449 Broadway joins a Richardsonian Romanesque building of 1888 by Van Brunt & Howe with an expansion that opened on November 8, 2009; six neighborhood branches serve the rest of the city.

history.text: Founded in December 1630 as Newtowne; it was renamed Cambridge in May 1638.
The college that became Harvard was founded.
George Washington took command of the Patriot soldiers on Cambridge Common.
Cambridge was incorporated as a city.
MIT moved across the Charles River from Boston to its campus in Cambridge.

name: Somerville
headline: A powder house, a hilltop castle,
and five Green Line stops opened in 2022.
meta: Somerville is a Middlesex County city of 81,045 people (2020 Census) just north of Cambridge and Boston. Triple-deckers, transit and 2025 prices, sourced.
answer: Somerville is a Middlesex County city of 81,045 people (2020 Census) on about 4.1 square miles of land just north of Cambridge and Boston, often described as the most densely populated municipality in New England. It is known for its triple-deckers, and since November 2023 three-unit buildings have been allowed citywide by right. The Warren Group counted only 72 single-family sales in 2025. Davis Square is on the Red Line, Assembly on the Orange Line, and five Green Line stations opened in 2022.
overview: Somerville was settled in 1629 as part of Charlestown and became its own town in 1842 and a city in 1872. Its hills played a part in the Revolution: British troops emptied the Old Powder House of gunpowder on September 1, 1774, setting off the Powder Alarm, and Prospect Hill was a Continental Army position during the siege of Boston, where tradition says Washington raised a flag on January 1, 1776. The Boston and Lowell Railroad opened in the 1840s, and in 1843 George O. Brastow laid out one of Somerville's first residential subdivisions on the south side of Spring Hill. Brickmaking, meatpacking and a Ford assembly plant, open from 1926 to 1958, followed.

The city is organized around its squares. Davis Square, a six-point intersection named for grain dealer Person Davis, gained a Red Line station in 1984, and the Somerville Community Path runs from there on an old railroad right-of-way. Union Square, named for its Civil War recruiting role, and Ball Square have Green Line stations that opened in 2022, and Assembly Square on the Mystic River grew from the old Ford plant site into the Assembly Row development. On Spring Hill, most buildings are wood-frame Greek Revival and Victorian houses of one to three units, with triple-deckers filling the remaining land in the early 1900s. The 2020 Census counted 36,269 housing units in the city.

Somerville adopted an entirely new zoning ordinance on December 12, 2019, its first major overhaul since 1990. The code sets standards for 23 building types, allows backyard cottages, requires most new developments to make 20 percent of their units affordable, and removed minimum parking requirements for most of the city, with maximums near Red, Orange and Green Line stations. In November 2023 the City Council made three-unit buildings legal by right citywide. The state housing office (EOHLC) approved Somerville's multifamily zoning ordinance on October 1, 2024, and the state lists the city as compliant with the MBTA Communities law. The city has since opened a five-year review of the 2019 code.

housing.text: Somerville is known for its triple-deckers. In November 2023 the City Council made any three-unit building legal citywide by right, without zoning board approval, replacing 2019 rules that required a new triple-decker to sit next to an existing one and include an income-restricted unit. Single-family homes are a small part of the market: The Warren Group counted 72 single-family sales in 2025.

villages.name: Davis Square
villages.line: A six-point intersection in northwestern Somerville, named a square in 1883, with the 1914 Somerville Theatre and a Red Line station opened in December 1984.

villages.name: Union Square
villages.line: The southeastern square at Washington Street, Webster Avenue and Somerville Avenue, once called Sand Pit Square, with Prospect Hill nearby and a Green Line station opened March 21, 2022.

villages.name: Ball Square
villages.line: A square on the Somerville-Medford line with a Green Line Extension station opened December 12, 2022.

villages.name: Assembly Square
villages.line: Named for a Ford assembly plant that ran from 1926 to 1958, on the west bank of the Mystic River between I-93 and the river, now the 45-acre Assembly Row development with an Orange Line station.

villages.name: Spring Hill
villages.line: A drumlin ridge in central Somerville roughly between Highland Avenue, Somerville Avenue, Elm Street and Willow Avenue, with Summer Street along its crest and the Spring Hill Historic District, listed on the National Register in 1989.

villages.name: Winter Hill
villages.line: The hill roughly north of Medford Street, with Foss Park at its base beside I-93, a Revolutionary War fort site, restored houses and triple-deckers, and Green Line stations at Gilman Square and Magoun Square.

rail.line: Green Line (subway, Union Square and Medford branches)
Fitchburg Line (commuter rail, in neighboring Cambridge)

commute.text: Somerville has no commuter rail station of its own; passenger rail service in the city ended by 1958, and the nearest stop is Porter in Cambridge on the Fitchburg Line. Rapid transit has returned in stages: Davis on the Red Line in 1984, Assembly on the Orange Line, and the Green Line Extension in 2022, with Union Square on one branch and East Somerville, Gilman Square, Magoun Square and Ball Square on the branch to Medford/Tufts. I-93 crosses the city on an elevated highway, Route 28 runs as McGrath Highway and Route 38 as Mystic Avenue.

places.name: Old Powder House
places.line: Built as a windmill around 1703 or 1704 and later a powder magazine, it overlooks Powder House Square from Nathan Tufts Park; both were listed on the National Register in 1975.

places.name: Prospect Hill Monument
places.line: A castle-like tower dedicated in 1903 atop Prospect Hill, a Continental Army position during the siege of Boston.

places.name: Somerville Community Path
places.line: A walking and biking path on a former Boston and Maine right-of-way from Davis Square, extended 1.9 miles beside the Green Line to North Point in Cambridge in June 2023.

places.name: Somerville Theatre
places.line: A Davis Square theater opened in 1914 that shows films and live performances.

places.name: Assembly Row
places.line: A 45-acre mixed-use development on the Mystic River, opened in 2014, with shops, restaurants, a 12-screen cinema and a hotel.

places.name: Mystic River Reservation (Draw Seven Park)
places.line: A DCR reservation of 329 acres along the Mystic River in Winchester, Arlington, Medford, Somerville, Everett and Chelsea, with field sports, picnicking, cycling and sailing at four riverside parks; Draw Seven Park is in Somerville, and its reconstruction was expected to last from late summer 2024 to 2026.

places.name: Somerville Museum
places.line: Run by the Somerville Historical Society in a 1920s Federal Revival building at One Westwood Road, at Central Street, with exhibits of local and historical significance and music and lecture series.

history.text: First European settlement, as part of Charlestown.
British regulars removed gunpowder from the Old Powder House on September 1, setting off the Powder Alarm.
Somerville separated from Charlestown and was incorporated as a town.
Somerville was incorporated as a city.
The Green Line Extension opened Union Square station on March 21 and the Medford branch, with East Somerville, Gilman Square, Magoun Square and Ball Square stations, on December 12.

Since November 2023, three-unit buildings have been allowed by right citywide, and the state lists Somerville as compliant with the MBTA Communities law.

name: Plymouth
headline: A harbor town of 1620,
with pine forest and ponds filling its western miles.
meta: Plymouth is a Plymouth County town of 61,217 people (2020 Census) on Cape Cod Bay, about 40 miles south of Boston. Homes, transit and 2025 prices, sourced.
answer: Plymouth is a Plymouth County town of 61,217 people (2020 Census) on Cape Cod Bay, about 40 miles south of Boston, and the largest municipality in Massachusetts by area. Founded by the Mayflower Pilgrims in 1620, it is one of the county's two seats. About 71 percent of its homes are detached single-family houses. Route 3 serves the town with six exits, and Plymouth's own commuter rail station has been suspended since 2021, so the nearest active stop is Kingston.
overview: The Mayflower Pilgrims settled here in December 1620, and Plymouth served as the capital of Plymouth Colony until 1691. The old town center keeps that story close to the water: Plymouth Rock under its 1921 portico in Pilgrim Memorial State Park, the Mayflower II at the State Pier, Cole's Hill, and Burial Hill above Leyden Street, where the Pilgrims built a fort in 1621 and 1622. Pilgrim Hall, opened in 1824 on Court Street, is the oldest public museum in the United States in continuous operation. Plymouth Colony merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691, and the town governed itself by open town meeting from 1622 until voters adopted a representative town meeting in 1953.

Beyond downtown the town spreads across about 96 square miles of land. North Plymouth grew around the Plymouth Cordage Company, once the largest maker of rope and twine in the world, and much of its multifamily housing evolved from mill housing; the company closed in 1964. West Plymouth filled with subdivisions in the 1970s, and South Plymouth drew new growth from the 1980s. Inland, Myles Standish State Forest has ponds and pine and oak woods, while Manomet and Ellisville Harbor sit along the Cape Cod Bay shore. Plymouth Beach, about three miles long, is the largest of the town's nine public beaches, and the town also holds the 81-foot National Monument to the Forefathers, dedicated in 1889.

Detached single-family homes make up 71.1 percent of Plymouth's housing units, according to its 2024 Housing Production Plan, and the town grew from 25,058 units in 2010 to 28,353 in 2021, with most new building expected in its rural areas. Because Plymouth is adjacent to Kingston, which has a commuter rail station, the state's MBTA Communities law treats it as an adjacent community that must zone for at least 2,807 multifamily units by right. On January 24, 2024, the Planning Board voted 4 to 0 to recommend Article 18 to the April 2024 Annual Town Meeting: a Multifamily Overlay District with four subdistricts, Cordage, Home Depot Drive, Plaza Way and The Pinehills, where, as drafted in January 2024, developments of ten or more units must make at least 10 percent of them affordable. The state now lists Plymouth as compliant. Cordage Park also has a Chapter 40R district, capped at 675 units.

housing.text: Plymouth's 2024 Housing Production Plan reports that detached single-family homes make up 71.1 percent of housing units, with attached single-family homes another 7.4 percent. As of 2021, 80.9 percent of occupied homes were owner-occupied, and the town's housing units grew from 25,058 in 2010 to 28,353 in 2021. The plan expects most new residential development in the town's rural areas, with recent projects in the south and at Cordage Park in the north.

villages.name: Plymouth Center
villages.line: The downtown, home to Plymouth Rock, the Mayflower II and Pilgrim Hall.

villages.name: North Plymouth
villages.line: A waterfront village around the former Plymouth Cordage Company, whose multifamily housing largely evolved from mill housing.

villages.name: Manomet
villages.line: A seaside village named for a Wampanoag village once among the Manomet Ponds, with White Horse Beach and Stage Point.

villages.name: West Plymouth
villages.line: The hilly, forested western section, where single-family subdivisions grew in the 1970s.

villages.name: Cedarville
villages.line: A neighborhood in the southeast of town, linked to Manomet by a local bus route.

villages.name: South Plymouth
villages.line: The southern part of town, which has drawn new residential growth since the 1980s; the Housing Production Plan notes recent projects there.

commute.text: Plymouth station at Cordage Park was suspended indefinitely on April 5, 2021, and is not on the current Kingston Line timetable, so the nearest active stop is Kingston station at 134 Marion Drive, with trains to South Station. Route 3 runs through town with six exits, and Route 44 ends in Plymouth. GATRA runs local routes including the Liberty, Freedom, Mayflower and Manomet Links, Plymouth & Brockton buses run to Boston and Hyannis, and a seasonal ferry sails from State Wharf to Provincetown.

places.name: Pilgrim Memorial State Park
places.line: The waterfront park at 79 Water Street with Plymouth Rock under its portico, the Mayflower II, Cole's Hill Burial Ground and views of Plymouth Harbor.

places.name: Plimoth Patuxet Museums
places.line: A living history museum at 137 Warren Avenue with the Historic Patuxet Homesite, a re-created 17th-century English Village, the Plimoth Grist Mill and Mayflower II.

places.name: Pilgrim Hall Museum
places.line: A granite museum at 75 Court Street, designed by Alexander Parris and opened in 1824, holding a Plymouth Colony collection.

places.name: Burial Hill
places.line: The hillside burying ground off School Street, with marked graves from 1680, including that of Governor William Bradford.

places.name: Myles Standish State Forest
places.line: A DCR forest of pine and oak with 13 miles of hiking trails, 35 miles of equestrian trails, camping and swimming at College Pond.

places.name: Ellisville Harbor State Park
places.line: A Cape Cod Bay shore park at 1861 State Road with a beach, meadows, red pine forest and harbor seals offshore in winter.

places.name: Plymouth Beach
places.line: The largest of the town's nine public beaches, roughly three miles long.

places.name: National Monument to the Forefathers
places.line: An 81-foot monument to the Pilgrims, dedicated in 1889.

history.text: The Mayflower Pilgrims founded the settlement in December, and Plymouth served as Plymouth Colony's capital until 1691.
After the fall harvest, the Pilgrims held a thanksgiving celebration with Wampanoag guests, remembered as the First Thanksgiving.
The Plymouth Cordage Company was founded in North Plymouth; it operated for more than 140 years before closing in 1964.
The National Monument to the Forefathers, 81 feet tall, was dedicated.
The present portico over Plymouth Rock was built.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Plymouth, MA?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, the median single-family sale price in Plymouth for calendar year 2025 was $654,450, across 606 sales. In 2024 it was $632,000, across 696 sales.

faq.q: Does Plymouth have commuter rail?
faq.a: Not at present. Plymouth station at Cordage Park was suspended indefinitely in April 2021. The nearest active stop is Kingston station in neighboring Kingston, at the end of the Kingston Line to South Station.

faq.q: Is Plymouth the largest town in Massachusetts?
faq.a: By area, yes. Plymouth is the largest municipality in Massachusetts by area, with about 134 square miles in total, of which about 96 are land.

faq.q: Which school district serves Plymouth?
faq.a: Plymouth Public Schools. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Plymouth, MA?
faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, Plymouth's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $12.55 per $1,000 of assessed value, the same rate for all property classes. No residential exemption is noted in the sources used for this guide; the Assessors' Office handles personal exemptions, such as those for seniors and veterans.

faq.q: Has Plymouth zoned for multifamily housing under the MBTA Communities law?
faq.a: The state lists Plymouth as compliant. As an adjacent community to Kingston, Plymouth must allow at least 2,807 multifamily units by right. The Multifamily Overlay District the Planning Board recommended to the April 2024 Annual Town Meeting had four subdistricts: Cordage, Home Depot Drive, Plaza Way and The Pinehills.

name: Braintree
headline: Saltbox houses on Washington Street,
and a station where three rail lines meet.
answer: Braintree is a Norfolk County community of 39,143 people (2020 Census), about ten miles south of Boston, where I-93 and Route 3 meet. Most of its housing, 64 percent, is single-family detached homes. Braintree station on Ivory Street is served by the Red Line and two commuter rail lines, and the Greenbush Line stops at Weymouth Landing/East Braintree on the town line. It is legally a city with a mayor and council, though it keeps the name Town of Braintree.
overview: Captain Wollaston first colonized the area, then called Mount Wollaston, in 1625. Braintree was colonized in 1635 and incorporated in 1640, and the old town once took in what are now Quincy, Randolph and Holbrook; Quincy left in 1792 and Randolph in 1793. The town counts John Adams, John Quincy Adams, John Hancock and General Sylvanus Thayer among those born in Old Braintree. The Braintree iron forge of 1646 is thought to have stood near Elm and Middle Streets, and water power on the Monatiquot River drew mills to South Braintree in the 1820s. The Old Colony railroad arrived there in 1845, making South Braintree a rail junction, while East Braintree grew at the head of navigation on the Fore River. Braintree became a city with a mayor and council in 2007, though it keeps the name Town of Braintree.

Washington Street carries much of the town's older fabric, including the Thayer Birthplace, built in 1720, and the Asa French House, built about 1699, both now in the town's historic district. A 1979 state survey found especially large concentrations of center-entrance Cape houses in East Braintree, along the Monatiquot, and Braintree Highlands was laid out as a street grid in the 1870s but built up mainly in the 20th century. Five Corners, on West Street, became a commercial junction after Route 128 reached it in 1931. Open space includes the Town Forest, Sunset Lake, Smith Beach, the Cranberry Pond Conservation District and Pond Meadow Park, shared with Weymouth, along with an 18-hole public golf course. The town site describes established neighborhoods, small clusters of new homes and several condominium complexes.

A 2024 town feasibility study counts 64 percent of Braintree's housing units as single-family detached and about 74 percent as owner-occupied. As a rapid transit community under the state's MBTA Communities law, Braintree had to zone for at least 3,769 multifamily units by right, 25 percent of its 15,077 year-round units. In December 2023 the Town Council voted 6 to 2 to create four overlay districts covering about 204 acres: two near Braintree station (one taking in the Marketplace at Braintree on Grossman Drive), one off Hancock and Pearl Streets in South Braintree and one beside Weymouth Landing/East Braintree, which the town's November 2023 compliance model put at 3,922 units. Projects of ten or more units must make at least 10 percent of them affordable, and the state lists Braintree as compliant. In March 2026 the Planning Board approved the site plan for 752 apartments on the former Armstrong World Industries plant off Plain Street, beside the restored Monatiquot River.

housing.text: A 2024 town feasibility study reports that 64 percent of Braintree's housing is single-family detached units and that about 74 percent of units are owner-occupied. Only 12 percent of units are studios or one-bedrooms. The study counts a 5.42 percent increase in housing units from 2010 to 2020. The town also lists several condominium complexes among its housing.

villages.name: South Braintree
villages.line: The old industrial center along the Monatiquot River, where mills developed in the 1820s and the Old Colony railroad made a junction in 1845.

villages.name: East Braintree
villages.line: The area at the head of navigation on the Fore River, with Colonial-era Capes along the Monatiquot; its rail stop is Weymouth Landing/East Braintree.

villages.name: Braintree Highlands
villages.line: Laid out as a street grid in the 1870s and built up in the 20th century; the Thayer house was built here in 1720 before its move.

villages.name: Washington Street
villages.line: The town's civic spine since a town house was built midway along it in 1829, with the Thayer and French houses and Town Hall.

villages.name: Five Corners
villages.line: The junction on West Street in South Braintree reached by Route 128 in 1931, where commercial building and gas stations grew up along the former highway.

villages.name: Elm and Middle Streets
villages.line: High ground north of the Monatiquot River where the earliest settlement grew, and the likely site of the Braintree iron forge of 1646.

commute.text: Braintree station, at 197 Ivory Street, has a Red Line platform, a commuter rail platform for the Kingston and Fall River/New Bedford lines to South Station, a busway and a 1,197-space garage. Weymouth Landing/East Braintree, on the Greenbush Line, sits on the town line with Weymouth. The seasonal CapeFLYER stops at Braintree on summer weekends on its way to Hyannis. I-93 and Route 3 meet in town.

places.name: Pond Meadow Park
places.line: A 320-acre park shared with Weymouth, opened in 1976, with a two-mile paved loop around a 20-acre pond and unpaved trails branching off it.

places.name: General Sylvanus Thayer Birthplace
places.line: A 1720 farmhouse at 786 Washington Street, birthplace of the West Point superintendent, moved here in 1958 and listed on the National Register in 1974.

places.name: Asa French House
places.line: A house built about 1699 at 766 Washington Street, now owned by the Braintree Historical Society.

places.name: Thayer Public Library
places.line: The town library across from Town Hall, on land acquired in 1953 and rebuilt in 1997, with more than 125,000 items.

places.name: Blue Hills Reservation
places.line: A DCR reservation of more than 7,000 acres and 125 miles of trails, with a paved accessible path on Old Route 128 off West Street in Braintree.

places.name: Sunset Lake and the Town Forest
places.line: Two of the town's recreation areas, along with Smith Beach and the Cranberry Pond Conservation District.

places.name: Monatiquot River and Rock Falls
places.line: The river through South Braintree, where removal of the Armstrong and Ames Pond dams began in 2023; a fishway bypass around Rock Falls is meant to let river herring reach Great Pond Reservoir for the first time in about 200 years.

history.text: Braintree, colonized in 1635, was incorporated as a town.
Quincy was incorporated from the original town, followed by Randolph in 1793.
The Old Colony railroad reached South Braintree, which became a rail junction as branches followed to Fall River in 1846 and Randolph in 1866.
The murders that led to the Sacco and Vanzetti trial took place in Braintree.
Braintree was incorporated as a city with a mayor and council form of government, and elected its first mayor that November.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Braintree, MA?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, the median single-family sale price in Braintree for calendar year 2025 was $725,000, across 214 sales. In 2024 it was $680,000, across 242 sales.

faq.q: Does Braintree have commuter rail?
faq.a: Yes. Braintree station on Ivory Street is served by the Red Line and by the Kingston and Fall River/New Bedford commuter rail lines to South Station. The Greenbush Line stops at Weymouth Landing/East Braintree, on the town line with Weymouth.

faq.q: Is Braintree a city or a town?
faq.a: Both, in a sense. It is officially named the Town of Braintree, but it has a mayor and council form of government and is considered a city under Massachusetts law.

faq.q: Which school district serves Braintree?
faq.a: Braintree Public Schools. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Braintree, MA?
faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, Braintree's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $10.06 per $1,000 of assessed value, commercial and industrial property pay $21.39, and personal property pays $21.33. No residential exemption is noted in the sources used for this guide; the Assessors' Office handles personal exemptions, such as those for seniors and veterans.

faq.q: Where does Braintree allow new apartment buildings by right?
faq.a: In four MBTA Communities overlay districts the Town Council adopted in December 2023, covering about 204 acres near Braintree station, off Hancock and Pearl Streets in South Braintree and beside Weymouth Landing/East Braintree. Projects of ten or more units must make at least 10 percent of them affordable, and the state lists Braintree as compliant with the law.

name: Barnstable
headline: Seven villages between two shores,
from the Great Marsh to the Hyannis ferries.
answer: Barnstable is the seat of Barnstable County, a town of 48,916 people (2020 Census) made up of seven villages that run from Cape Cod Bay to Nantucket Sound. Detached single-family homes make up 84.8 percent of its residential properties, and the town's housing plan counts at least 23 percent of its housing units as second homes. Hyannis holds the town's transit links: the seasonal CapeFLYER train from Boston ends at the Hyannis Transportation Center, and ferries leave Hyannis for Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard. U.S. Route 6 crosses the town as a four-lane freeway.
overview: Bartholomew Gosnold explored this shore in 1602, and English settlers arrived on June 4, 1638, making Barnstable one of the first towns of Plymouth Colony; it was incorporated in 1639. The north side still follows the Old King's Highway, Route 6A, through Barnstable village and West Barnstable, where the 1644 house that forms the original part of the Sturgis Library is the oldest building housing a public library in the United States, and the Olde Colonial Courthouse recalls a 1774 protest led by James Otis and Samuel Adams. Behind them, Sandy Neck runs about six and a half miles along Cape Cod Bay, backed by salt marsh, with Sandy Neck Light at its tip.

The south side faces Nantucket Sound. Hyannis holds the historic Main Street, a large natural harbor and the ferry docks, along with Barnstable Municipal Airport and the Hyannis Transportation Center. West along Route 28, Centerville reaches Craigville Beach, Osterville keeps the Crosby boatbuilding story in its historical museum, and Cotuit sits on Cotuit Bay, the home water of the Cotuit oyster. Inland, Marstons Mills takes its name from Benjamin Marston's fulling mill and keeps a herring run, kettle ponds and a grass airfield dating to 1929. Hyannis is also home to Cape Cod Hospital, the largest medical facility on Cape Cod, and the Cape Cod Central Railroad runs seasonal excursions from there to Sandwich and Sagamore.

Barnstable's 2025 Housing Production Plan counts detached single-family homes as 84.8 percent of residential properties and at least 23 percent of housing units as second homes; rental housing is 24 percent of the stock. Multifamily and mixed-use buildings are allowed by right on only two percent of the town's net land area, and accessory dwelling units were recently allowed by right in all zoning districts. The town had 1,485 units on the state's Subsidized Housing Inventory, 6.73 percent of its 2020 year-round units, against a 10 percent goal. In Hyannis, the Town Council approved new Downtown Hyannis zoning on February 2, 2023, replacing the Hyannis Village districts with seven form-based and hybrid districts that allow buildings of up to four stories and are meant to allow compact housing by right. Barnstable is not one of the 177 MBTA communities.

housing.text: Barnstable's 2025 Housing Production Plan executive summary counts detached single-family homes as 84.8 percent of residential properties, and reports that at least 23 percent of the town's housing units are second homes. Hyannis holds about one-fifth of all housing units; single-family homes are 59 percent of its units, and most of its units are rented. The plan names town-owned sites in Marstons Mills, among others, for new year-round housing.

villages.name: Hyannis
villages.line: The largest village, with the historic Main Street, the harbor and ferry docks, the Hyannis Transportation Center and Barnstable Municipal Airport.

villages.name: Barnstable Village
villages.line: The north-side village along the Old King's Highway (Route 6A), with a working harbor, the county complex, the Sturgis Library and the Olde Colonial Courthouse.

villages.name: West Barnstable
villages.line: A northwestern village on Route 6A whose land is largely Sandy Neck, the Great Marsh and the West Barnstable Conservation Area, centered on the West Parish meetinghouse of 1717 to 1718.

villages.name: Centerville
villages.line: A south-side village with the Centerville Historic District, the Centerville Historical Museum and Craigville Beach in its Craigville neighborhood.

villages.name: Osterville
villages.line: A village facing Nantucket Sound, with West Bay, the Wianno neighborhood by East Bay and the Crosby boatbuilding tradition.

villages.name: Cotuit
villages.line: The village on Cotuit Bay, midway between Falmouth and Hyannis, where the Cotuit Kettleers play Cape Cod Baseball League games at Lowell Park.

villages.name: Marstons Mills
villages.line: An inland village on glacial plains, with the Marstons Mills River, a herring run, kettle ponds such as Mystic Lake and Hamblin Pond, and saltwater access only at Prince Cove.

rail.line: CapeFLYER (seasonal weekends, Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day)

commute.text: Barnstable has no year-round passenger rail; the nearest year-round MBTA Commuter Rail stations are Middleborough and Kingston. In summer, the CapeFLYER runs weekends only from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day between Boston's South Station and the Hyannis Transportation Center, with stops including Braintree, Brockton, Wareham Village, Buzzards Bay and Bourne. The Hyannis Transportation Center is also the terminal for Cape Cod Regional Transit Authority buses, including the Sealine to Falmouth and Woods Hole, and for Plymouth & Brockton and Peter Pan intercity buses. From Hyannis, the Steamship Authority runs year-round ferries to Nantucket and a seasonal high-speed passenger ferry, and Hy-Line runs passenger ferries to Nantucket and a seasonal catamaran to Martha's Vineyard. Barnstable Municipal Airport in Hyannis has scheduled flights to the islands and Boston. U.S. Route 6 crosses the town as a four-lane freeway, and Routes 132 and 149 link Route 6A to Route 28.

places.name: Sandy Neck
places.line: A public barrier beach about 6.5 miles long on Cape Cod Bay, backed by salt marsh, with Sandy Neck Light's 1857 brick tower at Beach Point.

places.name: John F. Kennedy Hyannis Museum
places.line: A museum at 397 Main Street, Hyannis, on President Kennedy, his family and their connection to Cape Cod; hours change by season.

places.name: Sturgis Library
places.line: A library at 3090 Main Street (Route 6A) in Barnstable Village whose building is the oldest structure housing a public library in the United States.

places.name: Osterville Historical Museum
places.line: A museum at 155 West Bay Road, founded in 1931, with the Cammett, Parker and Jelly houses and more than a dozen full-sized Crosby wooden boats.

places.name: Hyannis Harbor and Main Street
places.line: A large natural harbor, the Cape's largest recreational boating port, beside the historic downtown Main Street shopping district.

places.name: Lowell Park, Cotuit
places.line: The summer home field of the Cotuit Kettleers of the Cape Cod Baseball League.

places.name: Cahoon Museum of American Art
places.line: A museum in the Crocker house at 4676 Falmouth Road (Route 28) in Cotuit, with American art from the 18th century to the present, including the folk art and painted furniture of Ralph and Martha Cahoon.

places.name: West Parish Meetinghouse
places.line: The restored meetinghouse in West Barnstable, built after the church split into East and West parishes in 1717, and still home to the West Parish of Barnstable.

history.text: Bartholomew Gosnold became the first European to explore the area.
Settled on June 4, 1638, as one of the first towns of Plymouth Colony, Barnstable was incorporated the following September.
Protesters led by James Otis and Samuel Adams interrupted court proceedings at the Olde Colonial Courthouse, now a museum.
The Cape Cod Branch Railroad reached West Barnstable, and a depot was built in the village.
Barnstable adopted a council-manager charter and was incorporated as a city on April 11.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Barnstable, MA?
faq.a: The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table reports Barnstable by village rather than as one town. For calendar year 2025, the median single-family sale price was $590,000 in Hyannis (131 sales), $664,450 in Centerville (142 sales), $665,000 in Marstons Mills (101 sales), $814,162 in Cotuit (68 sales), $885,000 in the row labeled Barnstable (60 sales) and $1,165,000 in Osterville (51 sales). West Barnstable has no separate row.

faq.q: Does Barnstable have commuter rail?
faq.a: Not year-round. The seasonal CapeFLYER runs weekends from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day between Boston's South Station and the Hyannis Transportation Center. The nearest year-round MBTA Commuter Rail stations are Middleborough and Kingston.

faq.q: Where do the island ferries leave from in Barnstable?
faq.a: From Hyannis. The Steamship Authority runs ferries to Nantucket year-round, plus a seasonal high-speed passenger ferry, and Hy-Line runs passenger ferries to Nantucket and a seasonal catamaran to Martha's Vineyard.

faq.q: Which school district serves Barnstable?
faq.a: Barnstable Public Schools. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Barnstable, MA?
faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, Barnstable's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $6.80 per $1,000 of assessed value, and commercial, industrial and personal property pay $5.94. Each property also pays its fire district's rate (FY2026, per $1,000: Barnstable $2.81, Cotuit $2.07, Centerville-Osterville-Marstons Mills $1.15, Hyannis $2.40 residential, West Barnstable $2.66) and a 3% Community Preservation surcharge on the town tax. Qualifying owner-occupants get a 30% residential exemption of $274,787 of assessed value, according to the Town of Barnstable.

faq.q: What has Barnstable changed in its zoning for housing?
faq.a: The Town Council approved new Downtown Hyannis zoning on February 2, 2023, allowing buildings of up to four stories and aiming to allow compact housing by right, and the town's 2025 Housing Production Plan reports that accessory dwelling units are now allowed by right in all zoning districts. Barnstable is not subject to the state's MBTA Communities law.
