name: Falmouth
headline: A village green, a seaside bikeway,
and the ferry to the Vineyard at Woods Hole.
answer: Falmouth is an Upper Cape town of 32,517 people (2020 Census) in Barnstable County, bordered by Buzzards Bay to the west and Vineyard Sound to the south. Its 2024 Housing Production Plan counts 22,817 housing units, about 86 percent of them detached single-family homes, with 30 percent counted as seasonal units. Falmouth has no rail station: Steamship Authority ferries leave Woods Hole for Martha's Vineyard, and buses link the town to Hyannis and to Boston and Logan Airport. The median single-family sale price was $804,000 in 2025, across 424 sales.
overview: English colonists settled Falmouth in 1660, and the town was incorporated in 1686. Its center has gathered around a triangular village green since 1756, when the meeting house moved there, and late Colonial and Federal houses still frame it with the 1796 First Congregational Church on its north side. Katharine Lee Bates, who wrote the words to "America the Beautiful", was born on Main Street in 1859. Woods Hole was raided by British forces in 1779, and the Falmouth Heights shore was bombarded by British frigates in the War of 1812. By 1872 the railroad had reached Falmouth and Woods Hole.

That rail line is now the Shining Sea Bikeway, 10.7 miles from Route 151 in North Falmouth to the Steamship Authority dock in Woods Hole, with a stretch along the water. Woods Hole is a working science village: the Marine Biological Laboratory dates to 1888 and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution to 1930, around the drawbridge at Eel Pond, with Nobska Light on the point above Vineyard Sound. Along the south shore, a run of closely spaced coastal ponds and necks leads east to the Waquoit Bay reserve, while West and North Falmouth face Buzzards Bay with harbors and public beaches such as Old Silver Beach.

The town's March 2024 Housing Production Plan counts 22,817 housing units in 2020, about 86 percent of them detached single-family homes and 30 percent counted as seasonal, with an estimated 62 percent in structures built before 1980. At 8.13 percent, Falmouth's Subsidized Housing Inventory is below the 10 percent Chapter 40B goal, and the plan sets a target of at least 80 affordable units a year, with strategies including pre-approved plans for detached accessory dwellings and housing on town-owned land. Town Meeting loosened the accessory dwelling bylaw in 2018, cutting the minimum lot size from 15,000 to 7,500 square feet, and since February 2, 2025 state law has allowed one accessory dwelling of up to 900 square feet (or half the main house, if smaller) by right in single-family zoning districts. Falmouth is not on the state's MBTA Communities list, although neighboring Bourne is, as an adjacent small town.

housing.text: Falmouth's March 2024 Housing Production Plan counts 22,817 housing units in 2020, up from 18,168 in 1990. An estimated 86 percent are detached single-family homes, and 70 percent are counted as year-round units, with 30 percent counted as seasonal; an estimated 62 percent are in structures built before 1980, and 8.13 percent count toward the state's Subsidized Housing Inventory. The plan aims to direct new housing to areas that are already developed and to maximize affordable units on town-owned land.

villages.name: Falmouth Village
villages.line: The town center on Main Street (Route 28), around the triangular Falmouth Village Green, a historic district listed on the National Register in 1996.

villages.name: Woods Hole
villages.line: The village at the southwestern tip of the Cape, around Eel Pond and its drawbridge, home to the Steamship Authority terminal, WHOI, the Marine Biological Laboratory and a USGS coastal and marine center.

villages.name: West Falmouth
villages.line: A Buzzards Bay village with West Falmouth Harbor and the West Falmouth Village Historic District, which includes the Quaker Meeting House and carriage sheds.

villages.name: North Falmouth
villages.line: The northwest village on Buzzards Bay, with two public beaches: Old Silver Beach off Quaker Road and Megansett Beach on Megansett Harbor.

villages.name: East Falmouth and Waquoit
villages.line: The south-shore area of necks between tidal ponds (Great, Green, Bournes and Eel ponds), with Hatchville to the north on Route 151 and Waquoit to the east on Waquoit Bay.

villages.name: Teaticket
villages.line: The village between Falmouth Village and East Falmouth, crossed by Route 28; south of the road, a neck between Great Pond and Little Pond runs down to Vineyard Sound and holds the Maravista neighborhood.

rail.line: CapeFLYER (seasonal weekends, Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day, in neighboring Bourne)

commute.text: Falmouth has no rail station. The seasonal CapeFLYER, weekends only from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day, stops in neighboring Bourne and Buzzards Bay on its way between Boston's South Station and Hyannis. Peter Pan buses run from Logan Airport and downtown Boston to the Falmouth Bus Depot. The Cape Cod Regional Transit Authority's Sealine connects the Hyannis Transportation Center with Falmouth Center and the Woods Hole ferry docks along Route 28, and from late June to Labor Day the Whoosh Trolley runs from the Falmouth Mall through Falmouth Center to Woods Hole. Steamship Authority ferries to Martha's Vineyard leave Woods Hole year-round, and the seasonal, passenger-only Island Queen crosses from Falmouth Harbor to Oak Bluffs in about 35 minutes. Route 28 runs south from Bourne as the town's main road, and Route 151 crosses the north of town.

places.name: Shining Sea Bikeway
places.line: A 10.7-mile rail-trail from County Road (Route 151) in North Falmouth to the Steamship Authority on Crane Street in Woods Hole, named for a line of "America the Beautiful".

places.name: Nobska Light
places.line: A lighthouse on Nobska Road in Woods Hole, a station since 1828 with its present tower from 1876, overlooking Martha's Vineyard and Nonamesset Island.

places.name: Waquoit Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve
places.line: About 2,700 acres of open water, barrier beach, marsh and upland in East Falmouth, with trails, a visitor center and boat-access campsites on Washburn Island.

places.name: Falmouth Village Green
places.line: The triangular green formed by Main Street, West Main Street and Hewins Street, the town center since 1756.

places.name: Woods Hole and Eel Pond
places.line: The village harbor of Eel Pond, crossed by a bascule drawbridge that opens on a posted schedule, ringed by the Marine Biological Laboratory and WHOI.

places.name: Old Silver Beach
places.line: A public beach on Buzzards Bay off Quaker Road in North Falmouth.

places.name: Highfield Hall and Beebe Woods
places.line: James Madison Beebe bought more than 700 acres in the late 1800s, after the railroad reached the Cape, and built Highfield Hall, now a museum; much of his former land is preserved as Beebe Woods, and the College Light Opera Company has played the Highfield Theatre every summer since 1969.

places.name: Spohr Gardens
places.line: About 6 acres of woodland garden at 45 Fells Road, with paths along Oyster Pond, open to the public free of charge.

history.text: First settled by English colonists in 1660, Falmouth was incorporated as a town.
The meeting house moved to the village green, which has been the town center since.
Katharine Lee Bates, author of "America the Beautiful", was born in Falmouth on August 12.
The railroad reached Falmouth and Woods Hole; its right-of-way later became the Shining Sea Bikeway.
The Marine Biological Laboratory was founded in Woods Hole, a village that had been a whaling station in the 1820s; the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution followed in 1930.

faq.q: How do you get from Falmouth to Martha's Vineyard?
faq.a: Steamship Authority ferries leave Woods Hole for Martha's Vineyard year-round, and the seasonal, passenger-only Island Queen sails from Falmouth Harbor to Oak Bluffs in about 35 minutes.

faq.q: Is Falmouth subject to the MBTA Communities zoning law?
faq.a: No. Falmouth is not on the state's list of MBTA communities. Separately, under the state accessory dwelling unit law in effect since February 2, 2025, one accessory dwelling of up to 900 square feet (or half the main house's floor area, if smaller) is allowed by right in single-family zoning districts.

name: New Bedford
headline: Cobblestones above the working harbor,
and the train back on Acushnet Avenue.
answer: New Bedford is a Bristol County city of 101,079 people (2020 Census) on the Acushnet River where it meets Buzzards Bay. Its downtown waterfront is part of New Bedford Whaling National Historical Park, established in 1996. The Warren Group counted 401 single-family sales in 2025. Since March 24, 2025, the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line has run from New Bedford and Church Street stations to Boston's South Station, and I-195 crosses the city.
overview: New Bedford was incorporated as a town in 1787 and became a city in 1847. In the first half of the 1800s it was one of the world's most important whaling ports, and in 1857 its harbor counted 329 vessels. The downtown historic district, 11 city blocks and part of a twelfth west of the waterfront, keeps Federal and Greek Revival buildings put up mostly between 1790 and 1855, including Seamen's Bethel and the 1836 U.S. Customhouse. Frederick Douglass settled in the city in 1838 and lived there until 1841.

When whaling faded, cotton mills took over, and the Wamsutta Mills were for a time the world's largest weaving plant. The housing that followed spreads out from downtown: the County Street Historic District, laid out in the 18th century, holds City Hall, the library and large houses in Greek Revival and Gothic Revival styles, while Acushnet Heights keeps wood-frame houses built for factory workers from the 1860s on. Buttonwood Park and its zoo sit to the west, and Fort Taber Park occupies Clark's Point, the city's southern tip on Buzzards Bay.

The state's MBTA Communities table counts 44,588 housing units in New Bedford in 2020, and the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 survey puts the owner-occupied share at 40.3 percent. In March 2023 the city published Building New Bedford, a housing plan that set a 90-day approval target for large multifamily projects, proposed smaller minimum lots and lower parking minimums (then two spaces per new unit), and proposed revisiting the rules on accessory dwellings, since detached ones were not then allowed. As a commuter rail community under the MBTA Communities law, the city needed multifamily zoning near its new stations: the City Council approved a transit-oriented district along Kings Highway, around Church Street station in the North End, in November 2024, and the state lists New Bedford as compliant as of October 21, 2026. A second overlay, the Clasky Common district along Purchase Street near New Bedford station, was proposed in early 2025.

housing.text: The state's MBTA Communities table counts 44,588 housing units in New Bedford in 2020, and the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 American Community Survey puts the owner-occupied share at 40.3 percent. The city's 2023 Building New Bedford plan counted 39,059 occupied units, 60.2 percent of them rented, and noted that triple-deckers are abundant and that surrounding towns have a higher share of single-family homes. Older neighborhoods mix 19th-century wood-frame houses with downtown commercial and mixed-use blocks, and The Warren Group recorded 401 single-family sales in 2025.

villages.name: Downtown and the Waterfront
villages.line: The historic district between Front, Elm and Commercial Streets and Acushnet Avenue, about 11 city blocks of Federal and Greek Revival buildings beside the harbor.

villages.name: County Street
villages.line: About 100 acres along County Street, roughly bounded by Acushnet, Page, Middle and Bedford Streets, with City Hall, the library and Greek Revival, Gothic Revival and Late Victorian buildings.

villages.name: Acushnet Heights
villages.line: About 20 acres around Clasky Common Park, bounded by Purchase, Linden and County Streets, with wood-frame houses built from the 1860s for factory workers and four 19th-century churches.

villages.name: Clark's Point
villages.line: The southernmost point of the city, where the Acushnet River meets Buzzards Bay, home to Fort Taber Park.

villages.name: Central New Bedford
villages.line: A 29-acre rectangle bounded by Acushnet Avenue and School, Middle and Sixth Streets, with 79 buildings, mostly commercial or mixed-use and largely Classical Revival or Romanesque Revival, including the 1908-10 Registry of Deeds and the 1915 Post Office.

villages.name: Howland Mill Village
villages.line: A 9.9-acre district roughly bounded by Bolton, Winsper and Hemlock Streets and Rockdale Avenue, with single-family cottages built in 1888-89 for the nearby Howland Mill on just two floor plans, and double-decker houses added in the 1920s.

rail.line: Fall River/New Bedford Line (New Bedford branch)

commute.text: Commuter rail returned on March 24, 2025, after a gap since 1958. New Bedford and Church Street stations sit on the New Bedford branch of the Fall River/New Bedford Line, which runs through East Taunton, Middleborough, Brockton and Quincy to Boston's South Station; sample outbound weekday trips on the current timetable take about 1 hour 40 to 45 minutes, and the timetable also shows weekend trains to New Bedford. Both stations are in fare zone 8 and have full high-level platforms; New Bedford station shares the Whale's Tooth lot with the SeaStreak ferry and has 150 spaces for rail riders, and Church Street station, in the North End off Church Street, has 355. I-195 crosses the city toward Providence and Wareham, Route 18 links it to the waterfront, and Route 140 runs north to Route 24 in Taunton. SRTA runs local buses, and SeaStreak ferries sail from New Bedford to Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket, with separate service to Cuttyhunk Island.

places.name: New Bedford Whaling National Historical Park
places.line: A fee-free national park in downtown New Bedford, with its visitor center at 33 William Street.

places.name: New Bedford Whaling Museum
places.line: Founded in 1903 by the Old Dartmouth Historical Society, at 18 Johnny Cake Hill.

places.name: Buttonwood Park Zoo
places.line: A city-owned, AZA-accredited zoo at 425 Hawthorn Street, with animals from five continents.

places.name: Fort Taber Park
places.line: A 47-acre park at Clark's Point with the 1857 stone fort, Endicott-era batteries and the Fort Taber/Fort Rodman military museum.

places.name: Seamen's Bethel
places.line: A white clapboard chapel in the downtown historic district, first built in 1832 and rebuilt after an 1867 fire.

places.name: Rotch-Jones-Duff House and Garden Museum
places.line: A house at 396 County Street, built in 1834 for whaling merchant William Rotch Jr. to Richard Upjohn's design on a one-acre block; a museum since 1983 and a National Historic Landmark since 2005.

places.name: Zeiterion Performing Arts Center
places.line: A downtown theater that opened on April 2, 1923 for vaudeville, passed to WHALE (the Waterfront Historic Area League) on December 31, 1981, was restored with WHALE funding for the first phase, and reopened on September 25, 1982; its facade was restored in 2014.

places.name: New Bedford Hurricane Barrier
places.line: Begun in October 1962 and dedicated on May 21, 1966, the barrier and its dikes run about 3.5 miles across the harbor and Clark's Cove, with a 150-foot navigation gate, and protect more than 1,400 acres in New Bedford, Fairhaven and Acushnet.

history.text: Incorporated as a town on February 23; it became a city on March 18, 1847.
Frederick Douglass settled in New Bedford, where he lived and worked on the wharves until 1841.
Construction of the harbor's hurricane barrier began in October; it went into operation in January 1966 and was dedicated on May 21, 1966.
The waterfront historic district was designated a National Historic Landmark on November 13.
Commuter rail service to Boston resumed on March 24, the first since 1958.

faq.q: What is the median home price in New Bedford, MA?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, the median single-family sale price in New Bedford for calendar year 2025 was $422,000, across 401 sales. In 2024 it was $395,000, across 412 sales.

faq.q: Does New Bedford have commuter rail?
faq.a: Yes. Since March 24, 2025, New Bedford station (536 Acushnet Avenue) and Church Street station (387 Church Street) have been served by the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line to Boston's South Station. The current timetable shows trains to New Bedford on weekdays and weekends.

faq.q: Is there a ferry from New Bedford?
faq.a: Yes. SeaStreak runs ferries from New Bedford to Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket, and the Cuttyhunk Ferry Company runs scheduled service to Cuttyhunk Island. Check the operators for seasonal schedules.

faq.q: Which school district serves New Bedford?
faq.a: New Bedford Public Schools. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in New Bedford, MA?
faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, New Bedford's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $10.95 per $1,000 of assessed value, a figure a March 2026 WBSM report also attributes to the city's Assessor's Office. Commercial, industrial and personal property pay a higher split rate. No residential exemption is noted in the sources used for this guide; the Assessors' Office handles personal exemptions, such as those for seniors and veterans.

faq.q: Is New Bedford subject to the MBTA Communities zoning law?
faq.a: Yes. New Bedford is a commuter rail community under the law. The City Council approved a transit-oriented zoning district around Church Street station along Kings Highway in November 2024, and the state lists New Bedford as compliant as of October 21, 2026.

name: Fall River
headline: Granite mills on a falling river,
a battleship at the foot of the hill.
answer: Fall River is a Bristol County city of 94,000 people (2020 Census) on the Taunton River and Mount Hope Bay, at the Rhode Island line. It grew into a leading U.S. textile city in the 1800s, and its housing still includes many 19th-century triple-deckers. The Warren Group counted 300 single-family sales in 2025. Since March 24, 2025, Fall River Depot station has linked the city to Boston's South Station on the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line, and I-195 and Route 24 meet here.
overview: Fall River separated from Freetown as a town in 1803, spent about 30 years named Troy, and took back its name in 1834; it became a city in 1854. The name comes from the Quequechan River, believed to mean 'falling river' in Wampanoag. A fire in July 1843 destroyed much of the town center, and the city motto, 'We'll Try', dates from the rebuilding. Mills followed the river's drop to the bay, and by 1868 the city had passed Lowell as the leading U.S. textile city. The 1847 Metacomet Mill is its oldest surviving textile mill.

I-195 divides the city into the North End and the South End. North of the highway, the Highlands ridge keeps houses from about 1840 to 1925 in Greek Revival, Italianate, Second Empire and Queen Anne styles, along with North Park, designed by the Olmsted Brothers. Below it, the Lower Highlands mixes Federal and Greek Revival houses with late-19th-century multiunit worker housing. On the waterfront, Battleship Cove and Fall River Heritage State Park sit beside the Braga Bridge, and to the south Kennedy Park, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, slopes down to Mount Hope Bay.

The 2020 Census counted 44,346 housing units in Fall River, and the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 survey puts the owner-occupied share at 35.3 percent. The city's Waterfront Transit-Oriented Development district, created in 2011 along the Taunton River, already set a minimum multifamily density of four units and allowed mixed uses; to meet the MBTA Communities law the City Council extended it north from Davol Street to North Main Street and from Walnut Street north to Wayland Street, and the state lists Fall River as compliant as of October 21, 2026. MassDOT has been replacing the Route 79 expressway on the waterfront with a grid of surface streets and a narrower, rebuilt Davol Street (the work was nearing completion in November 2025), and on July 24, 2026 it opened bidding to develop about 20 acres of former highway land on the river beside Fall River Depot, which the state says could support more than 1,000 homes; proposals were due October 21, 2026.

housing.text: Fall River's mill boom housed workers in thousands of wood-frame, multi-family tenements, usually three-floor triple-deckers with up to six apartments, and mill companies built more than 12,000 units. The 2020 Census counted 44,346 housing units, 7.5 percent of them vacant. The Highlands and Lower Highlands keep older single-family and Victorian houses, and The Warren Group recorded 300 single-family sales in 2025.

villages.name: The Highlands
villages.line: A historic district on a ridge above the Taunton River and Mount Hope Bay, with more than 300 structures built mostly between 1840 and 1925 and the Olmsted Brothers' North Park.

villages.name: Lower Highlands
villages.line: About 212 acres just east of downtown, roughly bounded by Cherry, Main, Winter and Bank Streets, settled by 1810 and partly rebuilt after the 1843 fire.

villages.name: Waterfront and Battleship Cove
villages.line: A North End neighborhood on the Taunton River where Battleship Cove and Heritage State Park sit beside the Braga Bridge.

villages.name: Flint Village
villages.line: A South End neighborhood known as 'The Flint', near Bedford and Quarry Streets.

villages.name: Globe Village
villages.line: A South End neighborhood around Cook Pond and Broadway.

villages.name: Townsend Hill
villages.line: A South End neighborhood around South Main Street and Bay Street, on the Tiverton, Rhode Island line.

rail.line: Fall River/New Bedford Line (Fall River branch)

commute.text: Fall River Depot opened on March 24, 2025, at 825 Davol Street, about a mile north of downtown near Route 79 and President Avenue, with 220 parking spaces, a full high-level platform and fare zone 8. Trains on the Fall River branch stop at Freetown, then run through East Taunton, Middleborough, Brockton and Quincy to Boston's South Station; sample outbound weekday trips on the current timetable take about 1 hour 40 to 50 minutes, and the timetable also shows weekend trains. A downtown station at Battleship Cove is a proposed, unfunded later phase. I-195 runs east-west through downtown, Route 24 heads north toward Boston's southern suburbs, and SRTA runs local buses.

places.name: Battleship Cove
places.line: A naval museum at 5 Water Street, opened in 1965, with the battleship USS Massachusetts, the submarine USS Lionfish and the destroyer USS Joseph P. Kennedy Jr.

places.name: Fall River Heritage State Park
places.line: A DCR park on the Taunton River with a visitor center, a mile-long boardwalk and trail, a picnic meadow and views of Battleship Cove.

places.name: Lincoln Park Carousel
places.line: A 1920 Philadelphia Toboggan Company carousel, restored by local vocational students and housed in a pavilion at Battleship Cove.

places.name: Kennedy Park
places.line: A 57-acre park from 1868 by Olmsted and Vaux, with ball fields above and woods running down to Mount Hope Bay.

places.name: Lizzie Borden House
places.line: The 230 Second Street house, now a bed and breakfast and museum with historical tours.

places.name: Freetown-Fall River State Forest
places.line: About 5,000 acres of DCR forest with about 25 miles of trails, including the walk to Profile Rock.

places.name: Quequechan River Rail Trail
places.line: A 2.3-mile, ten-foot-wide paved trail on a former railroad bed from Wordell Street along the northern shore of South Watuppa Pond.

places.name: Fall River Historical Society
places.line: A museum and archive at 451 Rock Street, with the Charlton Library of Fall River History and a large Lizzie Borden collection; as of October 2026 it is closed for an infrastructure project, so check its site for reopening.

history.text: Separated from Freetown and incorporated as a town; it was renamed Troy a year later and reverted to Fall River in 1834.
A July fire destroyed much of the town center, leaving more than 1,300 people homeless.
Incorporated as a city.
Fall River passed Lowell as the leading textile city in the United States.
On the evening of February 2, the worst fire in the city's history destroyed a large part of downtown.

faq.a: Yes. Fall River Depot, at 825 Davol Street, opened on March 24, 2025, on the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line to Boston's South Station, with trains on weekdays and weekends. A downtown station at Battleship Cove is proposed for a later, unfunded phase.

No residential exemption is noted in the sources used for this guide; the Assessors' Office handles personal exemptions, such as those for seniors and veterans.

name: Pittsfield
headline: A county seat around Park Square,
with two lakes and a state forest at its edges.
answer: Pittsfield is a city of 43,927 people (2020 Census) and the seat of Berkshire County. A city housing analysis describes its homes as mostly single-family houses and small two- and three-unit buildings, and The Warren Group counted 434 single-family sales in 2025. Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited stops at the Joseph Scelsi Intermodal Transportation Center, and the seasonal Berkshire Flyer runs from there to New York. US 7 and US 20 meet in the city, and the Massachusetts Turnpike is about 10 miles south in Lee.
overview: Settlement here dates to 1752, and the plantation of Pontoosuc was organized in 1753 before being incorporated as a town in 1761 and named for William Pitt. Park Square was laid out in 1790 on donated land, and the Old Town Hall, the county courthouse, the Berkshire Athenaeum and the First Church of Christ still face it. Late in the 19th century downtown pushed north along North Street, helped by an 1891 trolley line. In 1890 William Stanley Jr. founded the Stanley Electric Manufacturing Company here, and General Electric bought it in 1903. Pittsfield became a city in 1891.

Water and woods frame the city. Onota Lake, 617 acres and owned by the city, and Pontoosuc Lake are used for swimming, boating and fishing, and Pittsfield State Forest covers 11,000 acres with Berry Pond and 30 miles of trails. Herman Melville finished Moby-Dick at Arrowhead, his home on Holmes Road from 1850 to 1863. On West Housatonic Street, Hancock Shaker Village keeps 20 historic buildings, including a round stone barn from 1826. Downtown, the Colonial Theatre of 1903 reopened after restoration in 2006, and the Berkshire Museum, founded by Zenas Crane in 1903, holds more than 40,000 objects.

Pittsfield's homes are mostly older single-family houses and two- and three-unit buildings; the 2020 Census counted 21,738 housing units. On April 13, 2021, the City Council replaced the 2004 Downtown Arts Overlay District with a Downtown Creative District, which requires 20% of a building's units to be affordable but allows a waiver. In February 2025 the council allowed one accessory dwelling unit by right on any property with a one- or two-family house. One downtown conversion pairs the state's Housing Development Incentive Program with a local tax exemption: the former Berkshire County Savings Bank at 24 North Street is planned as Park Square Residences, 23 mixed-income apartments, and on July 9, 2026 it was reported to have received $4 million in state tax credits under that program. In August 2026 the Berkshire Regional Planning Commission began a housing production plan for the city, due to the state in May 2027.

housing.text: A 2009 city housing analysis describes Pittsfield's housing stock as relatively old, made up mainly of single-family homes and small multifamily buildings of two or three units, and counted 21,633 units citywide in 2008. In the Westside and Morningside neighborhoods next to downtown, more than 80% of homes were built before 1969, and many larger houses from the 1890s to 1930s have been divided into apartments.

villages.name: Park Square
villages.line: The downtown green laid out in 1790, ringed by the Old Town Hall, the county courthouse, the Berkshire Athenaeum and the First Church of Christ; its historic district reaches roughly to East Housatonic, South, North and Fenn Streets and Wendell Avenue.

villages.name: Upper North Street
villages.line: Late-19th-century commercial blocks along North Street, built as downtown grew north from Park Square after an 1891 trolley line.

villages.name: Westside
villages.line: The neighborhood just west of North Street, split by the West Branch of the Housatonic River, with denser older houses to the east and larger lots to the west.

villages.name: Morningside
villages.line: East of North Street between Springside Avenue and East Street, with one- and two-family homes, side-by-side duplexes and newer single-family homes on larger lots to the northeast.

villages.name: Tyler Street
villages.line: A district that MassDevelopment chose in 2014 as one of 10 pilot districts of its Transformative Development Initiative; its 2015 announcement names the William Stanley Business Park as one end of the district and describes the neighborhood as linking a future innovation district with Berkshire Medical Center.

commute.text: Pittsfield is outside the MBTA. Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited stops daily at the Joseph Scelsi Intermodal Transportation Center on its Boston section, with Massachusetts stops at Springfield, Worcester, Framingham and Boston. In 2026 the Berkshire Flyer ran from Pittsfield to New York's Moynihan Train Hall via Albany-Rensselaer on Fridays and Sundays from June 12 to September 19. The Berkshire Regional Transit Authority is based at the same center, with routes to North Adams, Lee, Dalton, Lanesborough and an express to Great Barrington. US 7 and US 20 meet in the city, and the Massachusetts Turnpike (I-90) is about 10 miles south in Lee.

places.name: Pittsfield State Forest
places.line: An 11,000-acre DCR forest at 1041 Cascade Street with Berry Pond, 30 miles of trails, an accessible Tranquility Trail and three campgrounds.

places.name: Onota Lake
places.line: A 617-acre lake owned by the city and used for fishing, swimming, water skiing and sailing.

places.name: Arrowhead
places.line: The 1785 house at 780 Holmes Road where Herman Melville lived from 1850 to 1863 and finished Moby-Dick, run by the Berkshire County Historical Society.

places.name: Hancock Shaker Village
places.line: A living history museum at 1843 West Housatonic Street on the site of a Shaker community active from 1790 to 1960, with 20 historic buildings and a round stone barn from 1826.

places.name: Colonial Theatre
places.line: A 1903 theater at 111 South Street whose restoration was completed in 2006.

places.name: Berkshire Museum
places.line: Founded in 1903 by Zenas Crane, with art, natural history and ancient-civilization collections of more than 40,000 objects.

places.name: Springside Park
places.line: A 246-acre city park at 874 North Street with Springside House, the Vincent J. Hebert Arboretum, gardens, trails, Springside Pond, a girls softball complex, a Little League field, a basketball court and an accessible playground.

places.name: Berkshire Athenaeum
places.line: The public library, whose roots go back to an 1850 library association, at 1 Wendell Avenue since 1975; its Herman Melville Memorial Room holds first editions, family letters and books from his own library.

history.text: Organized as Pontoosuc Plantation, after settlement began in 1752.
Incorporated as a town and named for William Pitt by Governor Sir Francis Bernard.
A town bylaw barred playing "baseball" within 80 yards of the meeting house, a reference found by historian John Thorn in 2004.
Incorporated as a city.
General Electric acquired the Stanley Electric Manufacturing Company, founded in Pittsfield by William Stanley Jr. in 1890; GE's workforce in the city later topped 13,000.

name: Great Barrington
headline: A Main Street on the Housatonic,
and Monument Mountain up Route 7.
answer: Great Barrington is a Berkshire County town of 7,172 people (2020 Census) in the Housatonic River valley. US 7 runs through its center as Main Street, and the town also takes in the villages of Housatonic and Van Deusenville. There is no passenger rail station in town; BRTA buses run to Lee and to Pittsfield, where Amtrak stops. The Warren Group counted 77 single-family sales in Great Barrington in 2025.
overview: The Mahican name for this stretch of the river was Mahaiwe, "the place downstream." Colonists settled here in 1726, the area served as the north parish of Sheffield from 1742, and it was incorporated as Great Barrington in 1761. In 1774 local colonists forced the Berkshire County court to close in protest of British policy, and in March 1886 William Stanley's alternating current system lit 23 businesses along Main Street. That Main Street still carries US 7 through the central village, where the Mahaiwe Theater opened in 1905 and reopened in 2005 as a performing arts center.

North of the center, the village of Housatonic grew in the early 1800s around textile and paper mills on the river; Monument Mills, which had 500 employees at its peak, closed in 1956, and the mill buildings are listed on the National Register. Monument Mountain rises along Route 7, with 503 acres and a 1,642-foot summit kept by The Trustees. To the east, East Mountain holds Ski Butternut and a state forest crossed by the Appalachian Trail. The Housatonic River Walk follows the river through downtown, and the W. E. B. Du Bois Boyhood Homesite, a National Historic Landmark, lies on the road to South Egremont.

Great Barrington's housing ranges from the Taconic and West Avenues Historic District south of downtown, where about two-thirds of the buildings date from 1890 to 1910, to recent nonprofit rentals. The Community Development Corporation of South Berkshire had Bentley Apartments, 45 affordable units on a former log-home factory site at 100 Bridge Street, under construction by February 2020, and with Way Finders opened Windrush Commons, 49 rental units in five buildings at 910 South Main Street, in June 2023. In December 2025 the state found the town eligible for its Seasonal Communities designation; the town planner told Town Meeting that seasonal units make up 12.71 percent of the housing stock. Voters accepted the designation in May 2026, giving the town up to 24 months to adopt any required zoning changes, and in an advisory vote declined, 94 to 31, to urge a residential tax exemption.

housing.text: Seasonal use shapes Great Barrington's housing. In December 2025 the Commonwealth identified the town as eligible for its Seasonal Communities designation, whose criteria include the share of housing units used for seasonal, recreational or occasional use. Voters at the Annual Town Meeting that opened on May 2, 2026 accepted the designation, which does not change local regulations by itself, and the Selectboard and Planning Board scheduled a joint meeting on related zoning changes for June 1, 2026.

villages.name: Great Barrington (central village)
villages.line: The town's central built-up area along the Housatonic River, where US 7 runs as Main Street and Routes 23 and 41 share it.

villages.name: Housatonic
villages.line: A village on the town's northern edge, bordering Stockbridge and West Stockbridge, with the river at its center and Route 183 crossing it; it grew around textile and paper mills.

villages.name: Van Deusenville
villages.line: One of the town's three named villages, with the central village and Housatonic; the Old Trinity Church stands at 4 Van Deusenville Road.

villages.name: Taconic and West Avenues Historic District
villages.line: A mostly residential National Register district (1998) south of downtown, bounded roughly by Main Street, Maple, West and Taconic Avenues and Castle Street, with 172 contributing resources, mostly houses, on about 117 acres; about two-thirds of the buildings date from 1890 to 1910.

villages.name: Risingdale
villages.line: The stretch of Route 183 south of Housatonic village, where the Rising Paper Mill, built about 1873 on the east bank of the river, was listed on the National Register in 1975.

rail.line: Amtrak Lake Shore Limited and seasonal Berkshire Flyer (in Pittsfield)

commute.text: Great Barrington has no passenger rail station. The Berkshire Regional Transit Authority runs Route 21 between Great Barrington and Lee and the Route 921 express between Great Barrington and Pittsfield, where Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited stops and the seasonal Berkshire Flyer runs to New York. US 7 is Main Street through the center, Route 23 crosses town west to east, and Route 183 serves the east side and Housatonic. The nearest interstate is the Massachusetts Turnpike (I-90). The rail line through town is the Berkshire Line, which the MassDOT Board voted in July 2014 to buy for future passenger service between New York and the Berkshires, with freight service to continue; passenger trains to Great Barrington ended in 1971, and their return remains a proposal. BRTA buses are fare-free through June 2027.

places.name: Monument Mountain
places.line: A 503-acre Trustees reservation on Route 7 with three trails to the 1,642-foot Peeskawso Peak, where Hawthorne and Melville once spent an afternoon.

places.name: Mahaiwe Performing Arts Center
places.line: The theater at 14 Castle Street opened on September 26, 1905, and reopened after restoration on May 29, 2005.

places.name: W. E. B. Du Bois Boyhood Homesite
places.line: A 5-acre National Historic Landmark (1976) on Routes 23 and 41, stewarded by UMass Amherst, with a path to a kiosk, a memorial boulder and the old house's foundation.

places.name: Housatonic River Walk
places.line: A national recreation trail along the river in downtown, a project of the Great Barrington Land Conservancy, open free in daylight from spring through fall.

places.name: Ski Butternut
places.line: A ski area on East Mountain with 22 trails and about 1,000 feet of vertical drop.

places.name: Lake Mansfield
places.line: A town-owned lake of about 30 acres, about a mile from downtown, with a swimming beach lifeguarded in summer, a 0.9-mile crushed-stone trail and a boat launch for canoes, kayaks and paddleboards; work on its parking, paths and play areas was substantially completed in November 2024.

places.name: Mason Library
places.line: The town's main library at 231 Main Street, opened in 1913; the stone base of an Alaskan totem pole placed on its side lawn in 1917 remains.

history.text: First settled by colonists, in the area the Mahican called Mahaiwe.
Incorporated as Great Barrington, after nearly two decades as the north parish of Sheffield.
Local colonists forced the temporary closure of the Berkshire County court in protest of British policy.
W. E. B. Du Bois was born in Great Barrington on February 23; he spent the first five years of his life at what is now the Du Bois Boyhood Homesite.
In March, William Stanley's alternating current lighting system lit 23 businesses along Main Street.

faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, the median single-family sale price in Great Barrington for calendar year 2025 was $575,000, across 77 sales. In 2024 it was $550,000, across 69 sales.

faq.q: Does Great Barrington have train service?
faq.a: No passenger rail station is located in Great Barrington. Passenger trains to Great Barrington ended in 1971; the MassDOT Board voted in 2014 to buy the Berkshire Line through town for future passenger service to New York, but that service remains a proposal. BRTA's Route 921 express bus connects the town with Pittsfield, where Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited stops and the seasonal Berkshire Flyer runs to New York (in 2026, Fridays and Sundays from June 12 to September 19).

faq.q: Which school district serves Great Barrington?
faq.a: Berkshire Hills Regional School District, the regional K-12 district for Great Barrington, Stockbridge and West Stockbridge. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Great Barrington, MA?
faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, Great Barrington's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $13.24 per $1,000 of assessed value, the same rate for all property classes. Great Barrington did not apply a residential exemption in FY2026; a January 2026 Selectboard presentation modeled adopting one, and at the May 2026 Town Meeting an advisory article urging the Selectboard to adopt it failed, 94 to 31. The Selectboard decides at its annual tax classification hearing, so check with the Assessors' Office for later years.

faq.q: What does the Seasonal Communities designation mean for Great Barrington?
faq.a: The Commonwealth found the town eligible in December 2025, and Annual Town Meeting voters accepted the designation in May 2026. It does not change local rules by itself; the town has up to 24 months to adopt any required zoning amendments, and the designation may open tools such as year-round occupancy restrictions, a year-round housing trust fund and zoning flexibility for undersized lots and tiny homes.

name: Auburn
headline: Auburn, where three highways meet
and the first liquid-fueled rocket flew.
answer: Auburn is a Worcester County town of 16,889 people (2020 Census), incorporated in 1778 as Ward and renamed Auburn in 1837. Its housing runs from 19th-century mill-village houses at Stoneville to bungalows and Colonial Revival houses of the 1930s and 1940s, and two former elementary schools became apartments in 2022. The Massachusetts Turnpike, I-290 and I-395 meet in town, WRTA buses run to Worcester, and the nearest MBTA station is Worcester Union Station on the Framingham/Worcester Line.
meta: Auburn, MA: 1778 town where I-90, I-290 and I-395 meet, with mill villages, Goddard's 1926 rocket site, 2025 Warren Group prices and FY2026 tax rates.
overview: Auburn was incorporated on April 10, 1778, from parts of Worcester, Sutton, Leicester and Oxford, and named Ward for General Artemas Ward; most of it had been Worcester's South Parish, first settled in 1714. In 1837 the Post Office complained that Ward was too similar to the nearby town of Ware, and the town became Auburn. Wellington, Dark and Kettle Brooks flow north and east through town, and in the 19th century they powered mill villages: Jeremy Stone built a brick woolen mill and worker housing at Stoneville in 1834, and Pondville's mills made yarn and satinets. The Norwich and Worcester Railroad began service through Auburn in 1840, and by 1900 a streetcar line ran from Worcester along Southbridge and Central Streets toward Oxford.

On March 16, 1926, Robert H. Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket from what was then the Asa Ward Farm. The site is now inside the town-owned Pakachoag Golf Course on Upland Street, where a granite marker beside the ninth fairway shows the spot; it was declared a National Historic Landmark in 1966. The town's commercial center is Drury Square, where Auburn and Southbridge Streets meet: one- to three-story buildings set back behind parking, with Auburn High School on the northwest side of Southbridge Street and the public library, Goddard Park and fire headquarters on the southeast side. The Auburn Mall, opened in 1971 at 385 Southbridge Street, sits on Route 12 near the junction of the Turnpike, I-290 and I-395.

The state approved Auburn's 2024 Housing Production Plan for July 9, 2024 to July 8, 2029, and certified it on July 21, 2025. Two former elementary schools have been redeveloped by Pennrose as mixed-income rental apartments: 55 units in the Mary D. Stone School at 10 Church Street, opened in May 2022, and 60 units in the Julia Bancroft School at 3 Vinal Street, whose opening was celebrated in December 2022. Under the state's MBTA Communities zoning law, Auburn is classed as an adjacent community that must zone for at least 750 multi-family units on at least 50 acres (the state counts 6,999 housing units in town in 2020), and the state's compliance list (as of October 21, 2026) includes Auburn.

housing.text: The state's MBTA Communities table counts 6,999 housing units in Auburn in 2020. The Massachusetts Historical Commission's 1984 survey found two-story, double-chimney multi-family worker houses and one-story duplexes of about 1860 at Stoneville, gable-end, side-passage houses built in large numbers around the mill villages in the 1880s and 1890s, a few triple-deckers, and bungalows and 1930s and 1940s Colonial Revival houses around the Center, Stoneville and Pakachoag.

villages.name: Auburn Center
villages.line: The civic center on Central Street, where the First Congregational church and first town hall replaced the burned meetinghouse in 1896 and the Merriam Library was built in 1910; bungalows and 1930s and 1940s Colonial Revival houses cluster nearby.

villages.name: Drury Square
villages.line: The commercial district where Auburn and Southbridge Streets meet, with low-rise shopping, Goddard Park, the library and fire headquarters, and the Auburn Mall within its study area.

villages.name: Stoneville
villages.line: A mill village in the north of town, built around Jeremy Stone's 1834 brick woolen mill, with two-story double-chimney worker houses, one-story duplexes from about 1860, St. Joseph's Church (1869) and a few triple-deckers.

villages.name: Pondville
villages.line: A mill village in the east of town where a saw and grist mill turned to yarn in the 1850s and made satinets and Union cassimeres during the Civil War.

villages.name: West Auburn
villages.line: A village around a tannery established in 1777 and taken over by the Warren family in 1807, with the 1825 West Auburn Schoolhouse at the corner of Central and Prospect.

villages.name: Pakachoag
villages.line: The hill area at the Worcester line, site of a 17th-century Christian Indian village, where bungalows and 1930s and 1940s Colonial Revival houses were built; the town's Pakachoag Golf Course holds the Goddard launch site.

commute.text: Auburn has no commuter rail station of its own; the nearest is Worcester Union Station, the western end of the Framingham/Worcester Line. I-290 begins in Auburn as the continuation of I-395, at a junction with the Turnpike, Route 12 and Route 20. WRTA Routes 27, 29 and 42 run from Worcester's Central Hub to Auburn Street, the Auburn Mall, Southbridge Street and Washington Street.

places.name: Goddard Rocket Launching Site
places.line: The spot where Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket on March 16, 1926, marked by granite beside the ninth fairway of the town-owned Pakachoag Golf Course on Upland Street; a National Historic Landmark since 1966.

places.name: Goddard Memorial Park
places.line: A park beside the fire department headquarters in Drury Square with a model of Goddard's rocket and a Polaris A-1 missile.

places.name: Auburn Historical Museum
places.line: The 1922 Tuttle Square School at 41 South Street, a Craftsman bungalow-style building leased to the Auburn Historical Society in 1999 and listed on the National Register in 2002; it houses the society's museum.

places.name: Eddy Pond
places.line: A 100-acre great pond and impoundment of Dark Brook, with a town-managed concrete boat ramp off South Street; fish include largemouth bass, chain pickerel and yellow perch.

places.name: Joseph Stone House
places.line: A First Period, one-and-a-half-story timber-frame house at 35 Stone Street, begun in 1729 with two bays added in 1790; listed on the National Register in 1986.

places.name: Auburn Mall
places.line: A single-level mall of 583,739 square feet at 385 Southbridge Street, opened in 1971 and owned by Simon Property Group, with Macy's and a Reliant Medical Group center as anchors.

history.text: Parts of Worcester, Sutton, Leicester and Oxford were incorporated on April 10 as the Town of Ward, named for General Artemas Ward.
Jeremy Stone built a brick woolen mill and worker housing at Stoneville; it became the Stoneville Manufacturing Company's cotton mill in 1839.
The town was renamed Auburn after the Post Office complained that Ward was too similar to the nearby town of Ware.
Robert H. Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket on March 16 from the Asa Ward Farm, now part of the Pakachoag Golf Course.
The Goddard Rocket Launching Site was designated a National Historic Landmark on November 13.

faq.q: Does Auburn have commuter rail?
faq.a: No. Auburn has no MBTA station of its own; the nearest is Worcester Union Station, the western end of the Framingham/Worcester Line. WRTA Routes 27, 29 and 42 connect Auburn with Worcester's Central Hub.

faq.q: Which school district serves Auburn?
faq.a: Auburn Public Schools, which serves prekindergarten through grade 12. Review its profile with DESE, and confirm school assignment for any address with the district.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Auburn?
faq.a: For fiscal year 2026 the town lists a residential rate of $14.24 per $1,000 of assessed value and a commercial rate of $15.83, according to the Auburn Assessing Division.

faq.q: Which highways meet in Auburn?
faq.a: The Massachusetts Turnpike (I-90), I-290 and I-395 meet in Auburn, where I-290 begins as the continuation of I-395. Route 12 (Southbridge Street) and US Route 20 also cross the town.

faq.q: Where did Robert Goddard launch his rocket?
faq.a: At what was then the Asa Ward Farm in Auburn, on March 16, 1926. The launch site is inside the town-owned Pakachoag Golf Course on Upland Street, marked beside the ninth fairway, and has been a National Historic Landmark since 1966.

name: Millbury
headline: Millbury, on the Blackstone:
armory village, mill brooks and a river path.
answer: Millbury is a Worcester County town of 13,831 people (2020 Census), set off from Sutton in 1813 and drained by the Blackstone River. Its housing is mostly detached single-family, with 19th-century mill housing in villages such as Bramanville. Route 146 and the Massachusetts Turnpike meet in town, WRTA Route 4 runs to Worcester, and the nearest MBTA stations are Worcester and Grafton on the Framingham/Worcester Line.
meta: Millbury, MA: Blackstone River town set off from Sutton in 1813, with the Asa Waters Mansion, mill villages, 2025 Warren Group prices and the FY2026 tax rate.
overview: Millbury was settled in 1716 and spent nearly a century as the north parish of Sutton. On June 11, 1813, Governor Caleb Strong approved the act that made the North Parish a separate town named Millbury. Water power set its course. John Singletary began running a mill in 1735 on Singletary Brook, which flows out of Singletary Lake, and in 1808 Asa and Elijah Waters built an armory on the Blackstone River that became the core of Armory Village and made bayonets and parts for Springfield muskets during the Civil War. The Blackstone Canal carried boats through the valley by 1829 and closed in 1848; a branch railroad reached Millbury Center in 1838, and the Providence and Worcester line came through in 1847. Josiah Holbrook founded the first formal lyceum here in 1826.

The center grew around the Town Common, at Main and Elm Streets, and the armory village on the north side of the Blackstone, where Asa Waters built a Federal mansion on Elm Street between 1826 and 1832 to a design by Asher Benjamin. The Greek Revival meetinghouse of 1828 at 20 Main Street is now the Millbury Federated Church. Rivulet Village, on Dorothy Pond, added 20 worker tenements in 1878, and the Cordis Mill expanded in 1914. Bramanville, on Singletary Brook, had seven factories by 1870 and kept its double-chimney worker housing; West Millbury had three wool scouring mills on Ramshorn Brook by 1875. The S & D Spinning Mill, built around 1753, is cited as one of the oldest continuously operated mills in the United States. Millbury was named a Preserve America community in 2004.

Millbury's 2019 Comprehensive Master Plan, prepared by BSC Group, counted 5,621 housing units (2012 to 2016 American Community Survey) and found residential use on 38% of the town's land. The plan names the Shoppes at Blackstone Valley, with more than 750,000 square feet of retail, restaurant and entertainment space reached from Routes 122A and 146, as the town's largest economic development project, and cites the Cordis and Felter's mills as examples of adaptive reuse. The state approved a Millbury Housing Production Plan under Chapter 40B on May 27, 2025, for the five years to May 26, 2030. Under the MBTA Communities law, Millbury is classed as an adjacent community that must zone for at least 750 multi-family units on at least 50 acres, and the state's compliance list (as of October 21, 2026) includes Millbury.

housing.text: The 2019 master plan counted 5,621 housing units, with 73% of households owning their homes and 27% renting (2012 to 2016 American Community Survey). About 26% of units were built before 1940, and the plan describes the stock as largely traditional detached single-family homes. It counted about 220 units, or about 4%, on the state's Subsidized Housing Inventory.

villages.name: Millbury Center
villages.line: The commercial and civic core around the Town Common, with the Academy (1832), First Baptist Church (1864) and temple-front Greek Revival houses.

villages.name: Armory Village
villages.line: The village that grew around Asa and Elijah Waters's 1808 armory on the north side of the Blackstone River; the Waters family's Federal mansion stands on Elm Street.

villages.name: Bramanville
villages.line: A textile village on Singletary Brook with seven factories by 1870, two-story double-chimney worker housing and the late Second Empire St. Charles hotel.

villages.name: West Millbury
villages.line: The part of town where residential building is least dense and the town's agricultural land is concentrated.

villages.line: A more concentrated residential area in the east of town, with Raymond Memorial Congregational Church (1934), Our Lady of Lourdes (1938) and early suburban streets such as Wheelock Avenue.

villages.name: Prospect Hill
villages.line: A hill north of the center that saw new residential building between 1915 and 1940.

commute.text: Millbury has no commuter rail station of its own; the Framingham/Worcester Line stops in neighboring Worcester and Grafton. Route 146 meets the Turnpike and Route 20 at Turnpike Exit 94 in Millbury, and Route 122A runs south from Route 146 to Millbury Center. name: Northborough
headline: Northborough, along the Post Road:
mill villages, an aqueduct and Mount Pisgah.
answer: Northborough is a Worcester County town of 15,741 people (2020 Census), set off from Westborough as a district in 1766 and made a town in 1775. Its center lines the old Boston Post Road, now Route 20, with colonial, Federal and Greek Revival houses and later subdivisions around it. I-290 has three Northborough exits, Route 9 crosses the south end, and the nearest MBTA station is Westborough.
meta: Northborough, MA: 1766 town on the old Boston Post Road, with Mount Pisgah, mill villages, 2025 Warren Group prices, the FY2026 tax rate and I-290 access.
overview: Northborough was the north part of Westborough until January 23, 1766, when it became a separate district; it became a town on August 23, 1775, and in 1807 annexed part of Marlborough. Its first meetinghouse went up in 1746 near the Post Road, where Cold Harbor and Howard Brooks meet. The Assabet River and the brooks powered grist mills, a fulling mill by 1749 and, from 1814, textile mills at Woodside; manufacturing began at Chapinville in 1832. Boots and shoes peaked in the 1860s, and comb and button making, begun in the late 1830s, was the leading industry by 1855. A railroad to Framingham opened through town in 1855 and was extended to Fitchburg in 1866.

Main Street is the old Upper Boston Post Road, and Milestone 33, at 143 East Main Street, is still engraved '33 Miles to Boston.' After the railroad arrived, the center spread southeast with a bank organized in 1854 (later the Northborough National Bank), a Second Empire town hall completed in 1868 and the Italianate First Baptist Church of 1860 at 52 Main Street, the address of the Northborough Historical Society. The Boston-Worcester Turnpike across the southern tip of town was rebuilt as four-lane Route 9 in 1930 and 1931, and the Massachusetts Historical Commission describes the 1930 Route 9 and Route 20 interchange as one of the earliest cloverleafs in the state. To the north, the Wachusett Aqueduct, built from 1897 to 1905, crosses the Assabet on its way to Marlborough, and Mount Pisgah rises to 715 feet, the highest point in town.

Suburban building after the Second World War followed the construction of I-290, which the Commission's 1983 survey saw as a pressure on the remaining orchards of Ball Hill and the farmsteads on South Street. As an MBTA adjacent community, Northborough must zone a district of at least 50 acres where multifamily housing is allowed at 15 units per acre. The 2024 Annual Town Meeting warrant carried a Multifamily Development Overlay District with two sub-districts, Southwest Connector and Downtown (about 47.94 and 11.29 acres on nine parcels in the Planning Board's February 2024 presentation), and a new Highway Business Southwest district for the area around Avalon of Northborough and Northborough Crossing. On December 10, 2024, the state's Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities found the 59.2-acre district, with an estimated capacity of 886 multi-family units, compliant with the law, and the state's compliance list (as of October 21, 2026) includes Northborough.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission's 1983 survey found seven surviving colonial two-story central-chimney houses, including the 1743 Samuel Gamwell house, and seven Federal double-chimney houses, from the period when brick came into use. Greek Revival two-story sidehall houses followed from 1830 to 1870, then Queen Anne and Colonial Revival frame houses, and post-war subdivisions came with I-290.

name: Paxton
headline: A hill town on the Worcester line,
with a state park and reservoir land.
answer: Paxton is a hill town of 5,004 people (2020 Census) in Worcester County, bordering Worcester. Its houses run from 18th-century center-chimney homes and mid-1800s side-passage houses in Paxton Center to bungalows and post-1945 suburban streets, and the town contains Moore State Park and large tracts of Worcester watershed land. Routes 31, 56 and 122 cross the town; commuter rail is reached at Worcester station.
meta: Paxton, MA guide: a Worcester County hill town with Moore State Park, reservoir land and Routes 31, 56 and 122. Housing, history, prices, taxes and schools.
overview: Paxton sits on high ground near the center of Worcester County: most of the town lies between 1,000 and 1,200 feet, and Asnebumskit Hill reaches about 1,400 feet, according to the Massachusetts Historical Commission's 1984 survey. The land was part of the Leicester and Rutland grants of 1686 and 1687, and the first confirmed settlers, Josiah and Jason Livermore, worked farms in the southwest from 1748. Paxton was incorporated as a district on February 12, 1765, from nearly equal parts of Leicester and Rutland, and became a town in 1775. It is named for Charles Paxton, marshal of the Admiralty Court, who offered a church bell in return; the bell never came. Through the 1800s the town made boots, and its boot shops' output reached $213,000 in 1875; a fire destroyed the main boot factory in the 1880s, the remaining shops soon closed, and dairying and market gardening carried the town's economy.

No railroad or streetcar ever reached Paxton, so the town grew along its roads: north and south from the meetinghouse, toward Worcester, and out along West and Maple Streets. Paxton Center holds the civic buildings, including the 1888 Town Hall and the 1899 Records Building on Pleasant Street and the Richards Memorial Library, added in 1926. Bungalows went up along West and Pleasant Streets between 1915 and 1940, and the population quadrupled after 1945 as automobile suburbs spread from Worcester. Large tracts went to Worcester's water supply: the Pine Hill and Kettle Brook reservoirs flooded lowland in the northeast and south, and the city owned about 1,590 acres in Paxton for watershed protection at the time of the town's 2003 open space plan. Moore State Park, a 400-acre state property on Sawmill Road, keeps the stone foundations of mills that ran from the 18th to the early 20th century.

Paxton's homes are mostly owner occupied: in the 2000 Census, 94.8% of its 1,428 occupied housing units were owned, according to the town's 2003 Open Space and Recreation Plan, and the state's MBTA Communities table counts 1,689 housing units in 2020. The town adopted a Watershed Protection District in 2001 and later required larger lot sizes, and the 2003 plan noted that about 98% of its land cannot support on-site septic systems for new development. Paxton has run its own municipal light department since 1914. Under the state's MBTA Communities law it is classed as an adjacent small town that must zone for at least 84 multi-family units, and the state lists it as compliant as of October 21, 2026. Anna Maria College, founded in 1946 and based in Paxton, closed at the end of the spring 2026 semester.

housing.text: Of Paxton's 1,428 occupied housing units in the 2000 Census, 94.8% were owner occupied, according to the town's 2003 Open Space and Recreation Plan. The plan recorded residential land growing 64% over the previous 30 years and an average of 16.6 new residential permits a year since 1995. The older stock, as surveyed by the Massachusetts Historical Commission in 1984, runs from center-chimney Colonial houses to gable-end, side-passage houses of the mid-1800s, mostly in the Center, and bungalows along West and Pleasant Streets from 1915 to 1940.

Commuter rail is reached at Worcester station, 2 Washington Square, on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line. Route 122 follows Pleasant Street through the Center, Route 56 runs north and south and Route 31 east and west.

name: Sutton
headline: Five villages, old mill sites,
and a granite chasm in the southeast.
answer: Sutton is a Blackstone Valley town of 9,357 people (2020 Census) in Worcester County, made up of five villages: Sutton Center, Manchaug, Wilkinsonville, West Sutton and South Sutton. The town's 2025 Housing Production Plan reports that 86% of homes are single-family detached houses. Route 146 and Route 122A run through town, and commuter rail is reached at Grafton and Worcester stations on the Framingham/Worcester Line.
meta: Sutton, MA guide: five villages from Manchaug to West Sutton, Purgatory Chasm and Route 146. Housing, history, home prices, property tax and schools.
overview: Sutton began as an eight-mile-square tract that the Massachusetts General Court granted to Edward Pratt and other proprietors in 1704, after a Nipmuc man, John Wampas, had deeded land in the area to Pratt. The Massachusetts Historical Commission dates the town's establishment to 1714, with settlement beginning around 1716 and the common and cemetery laid out in 1719. The town was much larger then: a parish set off in 1778 became Ward, later Auburn, and the northern section became Millbury in 1813. Through the 1700s Sutton was a town of dispersed farmsteads on drumlin hilltops, and the town had some of the county's most agriculturally productive soils. Population peaked at 2,718 in 1855.

Water power brought industry in the 1820s. David Wilkinson built a stone factory in 1823 at what became Wilkinsonville; the Blackstone Canal, opened in 1828, passed the village with a lock and basin until it closed in 1848, and the Providence and Worcester Railroad came through in 1847. On the Mumford River, investors from Providence bought the Manchaug site in 1826, and granite mills went up there in 1852, 1862 and 1868; the Manchaug mills closed in 1921. Sutton Center kept the civic role, with the 1829 Congregational Church and Rufus Putnam Hall, an 1824 school and Masonic lodge, while West Sutton grew along the Central Turnpike, opened around 1824. Sutton Center, West Sutton and Manchaug are each National Register historic districts. To the southeast, Purgatory Chasm cuts a deep rift through granite bedrock.

Sutton's 2025 Housing Production Plan, written by a town working group with help from the Central Massachusetts Regional Planning Commission and approved by the state in January 2026, counts 3,612 housing units in 2020 and reports that 86% of homes are single-family detached and 87% are owner occupied. About 15% were built before 1940. The town's Subsidized Housing Inventory stood at 55 units, or 1.55%, against the state's 10% goal, and the plan notes that recent building permits have all been for single-family homes. Public water reaches about 15% of the town's land through the Wilkinsonville, Manchaug and Whitinsville water districts. Under the MBTA Communities law, Sutton is classed as an adjacent small town that must zone for at least 181 multi-family units; the overlay brought to the Fall 2025 Town Meeting was recommended for parcels at 10 and 17 Galaxy Pass and 15 Pleasant Valley Road, and the state lists Sutton as compliant as of October 21, 2026.

housing.text: Sutton's 2025 Housing Production Plan counts 3,612 housing units in 2020 and cites American Community Survey estimates that 86% of homes are single-family detached and 87% are owner occupied. About 15% of homes were built before 1940, and the plan puts the average age of a home at about 56 years. Subsidized housing makes up 55 units, or 1.55% of the year-round stock, and recent building permits have all been for single-family homes.

villages.name: Sutton Center
villages.line: The civic village where Boston Road, Singletary Avenue and Uxbridge Road meet, around the common laid out in 1719; its 435-acre National Register district, listed in 2001, has more than 120 contributing resources, including the 1829 Congregational Church and an 1839 brick commercial block.

villages.name: Manchaug
villages.line: A textile village on the Mumford River, centered where Main Street meets Manchaug, Putnam Hill and Whitins Roads, with large stone mills and gabled, multi-family wood-frame worker houses; it was listed on the National Register in 2018.

villages.name: Wilkinsonville
villages.line: The village that grew around David Wilkinson's 1823 stone factory, where the Blackstone Canal had a lock and basin and the Providence and Worcester Railroad arrived in 1847; it also has a 1917 school building.

villages.name: West Sutton
villages.line: A turnpike village along the Central Turnpike from Manchaug Road to the Oxford line, in a 460-acre National Register district of 18th- and 19th-century houses, farmsteads, a church, a cemetery and an 1831 sawmill.

villages.name: South Sutton
villages.line: A small cluster of houses along Whitin Road, south of the Second Baptist meetinghouse.

commute.text: Sutton has no commuter rail station. Grafton station, at 1 Pine Street in North Grafton, and Worcester station are both on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line. Route 146, the Worcester-Providence highway, runs north and south through town, and Route 122A follows Providence Road, improved as a regional highway in the 1920s.

places.name: Purgatory Chasm State Reservation
places.line: A DCR reservation at 198 Purgatory Road with about two miles of trails to rock formations named the Corn Crib, the Coffin and Lovers' Leap; the Chasm Trail itself closes in winter.

places.name: Waters Farm
places.line: A farm at 53 Waters Road with a Georgian house built by Stephen Waters in 1757 and 120 acres given to the town in 1974; Waters Farm Preservation, Inc. maintains it as an open-air museum, and it was listed on the National Register in 1985.

places.name: Marion's Camp
places.line: The town beach at the end of Tuttle Road, with a pavilion, trails and a kayak launch; staff are on site from mid-June through Labor Day and a beach pass is required then.

places.name: Manchaug Mill #2 and #3 site
places.line: Town-owned mill ruins on the Mumford River, with granite blocks, a chimney foundation, a 1920 bridge and a stone arch bridge over the tailraces; a December 2024 CMRPC concept plan proposes an interpretive park with trails and a river overlook.

places.name: Sutton Town Common
places.line: The common on Uxbridge Road in the Sutton Center Historic District; the town's FY2026 capital plan sets aside $30,000 to restore its bandstand.

places.name: Edward Putnam House
places.line: A house at 211 Putnam Hill Road built in 1737 and pictured on the town seal.

places.name: Blackstone Canal Historic District
places.line: The canal corridor from Blackstone to Worcester, listed on the National Register in 1995, which passes through Wilkinsonville, where the canal had a lock and basin.

The northern part of Sutton became the town of Millbury.
David Wilkinson built a stone textile factory, the start of Wilkinsonville.
Investors from Providence bought the Manchaug mill site on the Mumford River; its mills ran until 1921.

name: Boylston
headline: A reservoir town between Shrewsbury and Clinton,
with the gardens at Tower Hill.
answer: Boylston is a Worcester County town of 4,849 people (2020 Census) on the Wachusett Reservoir, between Shrewsbury and Clinton. Most of its 1,823 housing units are detached single-family homes (74%, per the town's 2021 Housing Production Plan), and 67% of units were built in 1960 or later. Routes 70 and 140 cross the town, I-290 passes through, and commuter rail is reached in Worcester.
meta: Boylston, MA guide: a Worcester County town on the Wachusett Reservoir, home to the botanic garden at Tower Hill. Housing, history, prices, taxes and schools.
overview: Europeans first settled the northern part of present-day Boylston around 1705, near Sawyer's Mills on the Nashua River intervale, and permanent settlement followed after 1718, according to the Massachusetts Historical Commission's 1983 survey. The area became the second precinct of Shrewsbury in 1742, gathered a church and built its first meetinghouse in 1743, and was incorporated as the town of Boylston in 1786. Part of the town was set off as West Boylston in 1808. Sawyer's Mills was the industrial center from the mid-1700s, with saw, grist and fulling mills, a wire mill and, by 1855, a cotton mill employing 50. The Wachusett Reservoir, completed in 1905, flooded the Nashua valley and Sawyer's Mills with it: 302 people were displaced, 46 dwellings were moved or destroyed, and the town's population fell by more than half within five years.

The land falls from over 700 feet near the Shrewsbury line to just under 400 feet at the reservoir shore, and the town's roads radiate from the common in Boylston Center. There the granite town hall of 1830, paid for by the Boston merchant Ward Nicholas Boylston, now houses the Boylston Historical Society's museum; the public library is in a 1904 fieldstone building by the Worcester architects Fuller & Delano; and Hastings' Tavern, a brick five-bay building, went up in the center in 1818. The temperance lecturer John B. Gough built his Italianate house, Hillside, on Main Street in 1848. An electric streetcar opened along Main Street from Worcester to Clinton in 1898 and was gone by the 1920s; Main Street was rebuilt as Route 70 in the early 1930s, and School Street (Route 140) became the road to Shrewsbury. Morningdale, in the southwest, began to develop as a streetcar suburb of Worcester in the decades before 1915.

Boylston's 2021 Housing Production Plan counts 1,823 housing units, 74% of them detached single-family homes and 83.3% of occupied units owner occupied (2015 to 2019 American Community Survey). By the plan's year-built table, 16% of units date from 2000 or later. The zoning bylaw caps new development at 20 permits a year, allows buildings of more than two units only in the Mixed Use Industrial district by special permit, and, after a June 7, 2021 Town Meeting vote, requires 10% affordable units in developments of more than eight units. Boylston does not appear on the state's list of MBTA Communities. The 293.6-acre Hillside property on Main Street, a former Digital Equipment Corporation training center, now holds the municipal offices, fields and trails; a master plan for the site, funded by a state One Stop for Growth grant, explored community space, housing, small business, trails and conservation and was scheduled to finish in June 2026.

housing.text: The town's 2021 Housing Production Plan, prepared with the Central Massachusetts Regional Planning Commission, counts 1,823 housing units (2015 to 2019 American Community Survey), 74% of them detached single-family homes and 9% attached single-family homes. Of occupied units, 83.3% (1,499) were owner occupied and 16.7% (300) renter occupied. By year built, 15% of units date from 1939 or earlier, 18% from 1940 to 1959, 26% from 1960 to 1979, 25% from 1980 to 1999, 11% from 2000 to 2009 and 5% from 2010 or later. The plan lists 30 units, or 1.7%, on the state's Subsidized Housing Inventory, including the 24 rental units of Sun Bank Village on Heritage Lane.

villages.name: Boylston Center
villages.line: The civic center around the town common, with the meetinghouse sites, the 1830 granite town hall, the 1904 library, Hastings' Tavern (1818) and Italianate, Queen Anne and shingled houses of the later 1800s.

villages.name: Morningdale
villages.line: The southwest section along Route 70 toward Worcester, which began to develop as a streetcar suburb of Worcester before 1915, with many one-story houses and a 1926 Colonial Revival schoolhouse.

villages.name: Straw Hollow
villages.line: A district in the southeast corner of the town, the center of palm-leaf hat and straw braid making, which also developed as a dairy and orchard area, with a creamery and stock farm established in the 1870s.

villages.name: Sawyer's Mills (former)
villages.line: The mill village on the Nashua River in the northwest, the town's industrial center from the mid-1700s until it was cleared and flooded for the Wachusett Reservoir around 1900.

villages.name: Route 140 corridor
villages.line: The School Street corridor toward Shrewsbury and I-290, zoned in part as the 52.4-acre Route 140 Business District.

commute.text: Boylston has no rail service today: the Massachusetts Historical Commission records 19th-century lines that were discontinued or flooded by the Wachusett Reservoir, and the Worcester to Clinton streetcar on Main Street closed by the 1920s. Commuter rail is reached at stations on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line in other towns, including Worcester and Westborough. Route 70 (Main Street) runs from Worcester to Clinton and meets Route 140 (School Street) in town; I-290 passes through, with interchanges just outside the town at Route 140 in Shrewsbury and Church Street in Northborough.

places.name: New England Botanic Garden at Tower Hill
places.line: Nearly 200 acres at 11 French Drive, owned and operated by the Worcester County Horticultural Society, with conservatories, formal and naturalistic gardens, an apple orchard, trails and views of the Wachusett Reservoir.

places.name: Wachusett Reservoir
places.line: A 65-billion-gallon reservoir covering 6.5 square miles with 37 miles of shoreline, managed by the DCR Office of Watershed Management; running, walking and fishing (in designated areas only) are allowed, entered through designated gates.

places.name: Hillside
places.line: The 293.6-acre property at 215 and 221 Main Street, once a Digital Equipment Corporation training center, with the town hall, a gymnasium, two soccer fields, an 18-hole disc golf course, a community garden and walking trails.

places.name: John B. Gough House
places.line: The 1848 Italianate house at 215 Main Street where the temperance lecturer John B. Gough lived until 1886; it was designated a National Historic Landmark on May 30, 1974.

places.name: Boylston Historical Society museum
places.line: The granite ashlar town hall of 1830, built with a schoolroom below and a meeting hall above and paid for by Ward Nicholas Boylston, now the historical society's museum.

places.name: Boylston Public Library
places.line: A 1904 building at 695 Main Street by Fuller & Delano, given by Salome E. White in memory of her mother, Harriet Sawyer, on the site of the 1841 Center School.

places.name: Harrington Park
places.line: A town park at 320 Sewall Street with a short walking trail and the only public access to the shoreline of Sewall Pond.

places.name: Manor Park
places.line: A Morningdale park reached by Orient Street off Route 70 and then Midland Street, with three baseball diamonds and a playground.

history.text: Europeans began settling near Sawyer's Mills on the Nashua River intervale, around this year; permanent occupation followed after 1718.
The second precinct of Shrewsbury, organized in 1742, was incorporated as the town of Boylston.
The cornerstone of the granite town hall was laid on August 21, and the building was finished that year.
The Wachusett Reservoir was completed, flooding Sawyer's Mills; 302 people were displaced and 46 dwellings were moved or destroyed in Boylston.
The Worcester County Horticultural Society's garden at Tower Hill had its beginnings.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Boylston, MA?
faq.a: The median single-family sale price in Boylston was $583,500 in calendar year 2025, across 46 sales, up from $580,000 across 37 sales in 2024, according to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town report. The same report gives a condominium median of $625,800 across 30 sales in 2025, up from $565,000 across 13 sales in 2024.

faq.q: Does Boylston have commuter rail?
faq.a: No. Boylston has no rail service. Commuter rail is reached at stations on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line in other towns, including Worcester and Westborough.

faq.q: Which school district serves Boylston?
faq.a: Boylston is served by the Berlin-Boylston Regional School District, which DESE lists as a PK to 12 district with three schools; Tahanto Regional Middle/High School is run jointly with Berlin. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Boylston?
faq.a: Boylston's FY2026 tax rate is $13.58 per $1,000 of assessed value, according to the town Assessors' Office. The town uses one rate for all property classes.

faq.q: Is Boylston the same town as West Boylston?
faq.a: No. West Boylston was set off from Boylston in 1808 and is a separate neighboring town, with its own town government and tax rate.

faq.q: Can you walk or fish at the Wachusett Reservoir?
faq.a: Yes, in designated areas. The DCR Office of Watershed Management allows running, walking and fishing in designated areas from one hour before sunrise to one hour after sunset, with entry through designated gates and parking at several of them; boating, swimming, dogs and horses are not allowed, and biking is limited to allowed routes.

Town's 2021 Housing Production Plan (mass.gov/doc/boylston-plan/download, with CMRPC, 2015 to 2019 ACS data) for housing units, structure type, tenure, year built, zoning, the 20-permit growth cap, inclusionary zoning (June 7, 2021), SHI (30 units, 1.7%), Sun Bank Village and the Route 140 Business District (52.4 acres). The overview's '16% built since 2000' is the sum of the plan's 11% and 5% rows; its own text says homes of the past two decades are 'only 5%' while its table gives 11% for 2000 to 2009 and 5% for 2010 or later, and the table is used. Gough House: Wikipedia (215 Main Street, 1848, Italianate, NRHP March 19, 1974, NHL May 30, 1974, Shepherd Knapp School, DEC in the 1980s; Wikipedia says the Boylston Historical Society controls the house).
